# Welcome {-}

How many participants does a study need to answer its research question? This tutorial helps students and researchers understand, justify and critically assess sample size calculations through worked examples, interactive activities and [simulations](#statistical-simulation).

Although the examples are clinical, the principles of justifying assumptions, choosing a target difference, and examining power and precision also apply in psychology, education, and other quantitative disciplines [@lakens2022]. The tutorial is a suitable starting point for learning these principles and planning comparisons of two independent groups with a continuous or binary outcome, provided the calculation’s assumptions match your study. Later chapters introduce other planning goals and help you recognize when a different method is needed. For factorial experiments and repeated-measures ANOVA, including designs common in psychology, *[Power Analysis with Superpower](https://aaroncaldwell.us/SuperpowerBook/)* provides more directly applicable examples and simulations [@superpowerbook2022]. Studies involving multilevel models, prediction, or time-to-event outcomes need guidance matched to those analyses; the chapter [Study designs and testing strategies](#study-designs) points you toward relevant resources. What counts as a worthwhile difference should also reflect your field and research question.

## How to use this tutorial {-}

The tutorial can be read selectively according to your study and learning needs. Chapters 1–3 provide a starting point for planning, calculating and reporting sample size for a basic two-arm trial. Chapters 4–8 are Extensions covering additional planning questions, methods and study designs. The roadmap and chapter learning outcomes can help you choose the relevant chapters. The glossary, common questions and worked examples provide support whenever you need it.

```{r tutorial-roadmap, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
roadmap <- paste(readLines("../figures/tutorial-roadmap.svg",
  encoding="UTF-8", warn=FALSE), collapse="\n")
# Numeric entities keep SVG text intact when R uses a non-UTF-8 locale.
roadmap <- paste(vapply(utf8ToInt(enc2utf8(roadmap)), function(cp) {
  if (cp > 127L) sprintf("&#%d;", cp) else intToUtf8(cp)
}, character(1)), collapse="")
cat('<figure class="tutorial-roadmap">',
    roadmap, '</figure>')
```

Chapter quizzes and the [cumulative quiz](#cumulative-quiz) help you check your understanding. The [activity walkthroughs](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/student-materials/activity-walkthroughs.html) provide additional guidance when needed.

The three core chapters develop one [sample size calculation report](#reporting).

[Flashcards](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/student-materials/flashcards/index.html) are available as Core and Complete tutorial decks, with a [question-and-answer preview](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/student-materials/flashcards/cards.html) and Anki/Quizlet downloads.

The overarching learning outcome is to critically appraise how a medical study justifies its sample size and judge whether its assumptions, methods and results support its conclusions. The outcomes below develop the knowledge and skills needed for that appraisal.

::: {.learning-goals .core-outcomes}
## Learning outcomes for Core material {#core-route .unnumbered .core-heading}

The linked sections should help you develop a sample size justification for a basic two-arm trial. By the end, you should be able to:

- [Define a clinical question and justify assumptions](#clinical-question), distinguishing the [difference observed in previous data](#expected-difference), [target difference](#target-difference) and [clinical threshold](#clinical-threshold).
- [Explain Type I error probability, Type II error probability and power](#power).
- Compare [one simulated trial and repeated trials](#activity-1-one-study-then-many) to distinguish [sample estimates](#sample-estimate) from [population parameters](#population-parameter), then explain what changes with a larger sample.
- [Calculate sample size for two proportions or two means](#calculations) and [adjust recruitment for expected losses](#account-for-expected-losses), distinguishing analyzable counts from recruitment counts.
- Compare calculations after changing one [assumption](#calculations) and justify the inputs selected for the report.
- [Write a short sample size justification](#write-a-sample-size-justification) recording assumptions, calculation and recruitment, using [your continuing report](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/assumptions_report/?stage=question).

:::

::: {.learning-goals .advanced-outcomes}
## Learning outcomes for Extensions {#advanced-route .unnumbered .advanced-heading}

The Extensions address different study questions and methods. Their learning outcomes are to:

- Plan a [prevalence estimate](#prevalence) or [population mean estimate](#plan-for-precision) for a useful confidence interval width, and [interpret intervals clinically](#interpret-a-confidence-interval-clinically).
- Distinguish [an observed significance boundary from planned power](#critical-observed-difference) and explore [sampling distributions and error regions](#alpha-beta).
- [Read power curves](#curves), assess [plausible alternative assumptions](#stress-test-the-study-plan), and explain the consequences of [low power](#what-if-the-study-is-too-small-for-its-purpose).
- [Build a simulated clinical trial](#simulation) to examine power, coverage and precision, accounting for [Monte Carlo uncertainty](#monte-carlo-error).
- Assess [existing-data reuse](#dataset-reuse), [rare-disease constraints](#rare-diseases), and the information needed for decisions in a [pilot or feasibility study](#pilot-feasibility).
- Recognize [study designs that need another method](#study-designs), including paired measurements and prediction models.
- Explain how [multiple comparisons](#multiple-outcomes-comparisons), [interim analyses](#interim-analyses-stopping) and [sample-size re-estimation](#sample-size-re-estimation) affect planning and reporting.
- [Reproduce calculations and simulations](#appendix) with their assumptions and methods documented.

:::


# Research question and power {#clinical-question .core-heading}

::: {.learning-goals .core-outcomes}
After this chapter, you should be able to:

- Specify a clinical question, outcome, design and planned comparison.
- Distinguish a difference observed in earlier data, a calculation target and a clinical threshold.
- Explain Type I and Type II error probabilities and power under specified assumptions.
- Compare one trial, repeated trials and a larger sample to explain sampling variability and power.
:::

## The neuropathic pain trial: how many patients do you need? {#the-chronic-pain-study-how-many-patients-do-we-need .core-heading}

Suppose you are a clinician caring for people with neuropathic pain associated with diabetic peripheral neuropathy. You identify a promising drug candidate, neravixa—a fictional medicine for this example—and want to investigate whether it helps more patients achieve pain relief than duloxetine, an established treatment [@emaduloxetine].

A small [pilot study](#pilot-study) found that 7 of 10 patients receiving neravixa achieved pain relief, compared with 3 of 10 receiving duloxetine: 70% versus 30%, an observed difference of 40 [percentage points](#percentage-points). This is a promising result, but the difference is uncertain because so few patients were studied.

You plan a larger trial in which eligible patients will be randomly assigned in equal numbers to neravixa or duloxetine. The [primary outcome](#primary-outcome) at four weeks is [binary](#binary-outcome): each patient either achieved measurable pain relief or did not, using the same assessment in both groups. Subsequent examples use the shorter labels “achieved pain relief” and “did not achieve pain relief.” Throughout this case, neravixa is the novel treatment and duloxetine is the standard treatment.

Figure \@ref(fig:pain-pilot-patients) illustrates these pilot results.

```{r pain-pilot-patients, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.7, fig.cap="Illustration of the hypothetical pilot: ten patients per treatment group start with pain. The counts describe this small pilot sample.", fig.alt="Two treatment groups: standard treatment on the left and novel treatment on the right. Each is shown before treatment and after a downward arrow marking four weeks. All ten patients in each group start red, indicating pain. In the standard-treatment group, three of ten become green with raised arms, indicating reported pain relief, and seven remain red. In the novel-treatment group, seven of ten become green and three remain red. Pain relief is reported by 30% with standard treatment and 70% with novel treatment."}
draw_pain_pilot_patients()
```

How many patients would this trial need to have a high probability of detecting a clinically worthwhile difference? In this tutorial, you will work through the decisions behind that calculation and explore the results that different repetitions of the trial could produce.

This chapter focuses on two-arm randomized superiority trials: patients are assigned by chance to one of two treatment groups, and the aim is to investigate whether one treatment performs better than the other. The core calculations cover binary and continuous outcomes. The separate [estimation chapter](#estimation-planning) uses a precision target; later chapters address other designs.

The following sections develop the question and assumptions that determine the calculation in Chapter 2.

## Why does sample size matter? {#what-should-this-study-establish .core-heading}

A sample size calculation helps assess what the planned study could establish under its assumptions. Too few patients may leave a clinically worthwhile difference undetected; unnecessary recruitment adds participant burden and time. The proposed trial needs a meaningful question, sufficient power for its intended comparison, and a feasible recruitment plan.

### Ethical review and the study protocol {.core-heading}

A scientifically sound study is an ethical requirement. The Declaration of Helsinki sets out international ethical principles, including scientific validity, a justified [study protocol](#study-protocol), and prior [research ethics committee](#research-ethics-committee) review [@wmahelsinki2024]. Your protocol should explain the proposed sample size, the evidence behind its assumptions, and the information expected in relation to participants' burden and risk.

For clinical trials of medicines, the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) provides a shared statistical framework used worldwide in its [E9 guideline](#ich-e9). Its sample-size guidance calls for an explicit outcome, target difference, analysis, error probabilities and assumptions, with sensitivity to uncertainty considered [@iche91998].

Review procedures depend on the country and study type. Your institution's research office or ethics committee should help identify the applicable requirements. The following are regional and national examples:

- European Union: clinical trials of medicines within the scope of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 require scientific and ethical review; ethics committees operate under the law of the relevant member state [@ecethicsreview]. Other study types follow their applicable frameworks.
- Netherlands: research within the [Medical Research Involving Human Subjects Act (WMO)](#wmo) framework is reviewed by an accredited [medical research ethics committee (METC)](#metc) or the [Central Committee on Research Involving Human Subjects (CCMO)](#ccmo), as applicable [@ccmowmo].
- United States: an [institutional review board (IRB)](#institutional-review-board) reviews studies subject to the relevant human-participant protections. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) requirements apply to covered clinical investigations; Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) regulations apply to covered research conducted or supported by HHS [@fdairb2025; @hhsresearchreview].

<span id="ethics-sample-size"></span>

## Defining the research question and study design {#how-do-you-determine-the-minimum-required-sample-size .core-heading}

A sample size calculation supports these scientific and ethical judgments when it addresses a clearly defined research question. PICO identifies the Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcome, including the assessment time [@richardson1995]. For the neuropathic pain trial:

| PICO element | Specification |
|:--|:--|
| Population | Adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes mellitus, bilateral lower-extremity pain attributable to diabetic peripheral neuropathy for at least one year, and body mass index (BMI) ≥18 and <40 kg/m². |
| Intervention | neravixa, the novel treatment. |
| Comparator | duloxetine, the standard treatment. |
| Outcome | Achieved pain relief at four weeks: yes or no, assessed in the same way in both groups. |

Table: (\#tab:pain-pico) The clinical question for the neuropathic pain trial, specified using PICO.

Participants will be individually randomized in a 1:1 ratio to two [independent groups](#independent-groups). Each person contributes one outcome. The comparison concerns the absolute difference between the groups' pain-relief percentages. The planned analysis compares two independent proportions using a [two-sided test](#two-sided-test).

Guidance for the study design helps identify decisions to document before choosing calculation inputs [@fong2026; @wang2020]. For randomized trials, [SPIRIT](#spirit) 2025 covers protocols and [CONSORT](#consort) 2025 covers reporting results [@spiritconsort2025]. The chapter [Study designs and testing strategies](#study-designs) links to guidance for other designs, including [STROBE](#strobe) for observational studies and [STARD](#stard) for diagnostic accuracy.

The map provides an overview of the remaining planning decisions. Its short explanations link to the sections where each decision is developed.

knitr::asis_output(render_question_map())
```

## Pilot findings, target difference, and clinical importance {#what-do-we-expect-what-will-we-plan-for-and-what-matters-clinically .core-heading}

The pilot findings provide a starting point for planning the larger trial. Three quantities help organize the reasoning: the difference observed in the pilot, the target difference used in the calculation, and the clinical threshold. All three concern differences between groups.

The [difference observed in the pilot](#expected-difference) is 40 percentage points: 70% achieved pain relief with neravixa, compared with 30% with duloxetine. This describes the patients in that small study. Another pilot could produce a different result. These findings should therefore be considered alongside other relevant evidence, including differences in pain severity, background treatment and assessment time.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-pilot-effect">
<summary>Common misconception: the treatment difference observed in a pilot is the true population difference</summary>

If another pilot found relief in 8 of 10 patients receiving neravixa and 3 of 10 receiving duloxetine, its observed difference would be 50 percentage points. That new sample result would add evidence to the planning decision. The target difference would still need justification using all relevant findings and clinical importance [@albers2018].

</details>

The [target difference](#target-difference) is the population difference at which the sample size calculation evaluates [power](#statistical-power). The trial is planned for a target difference of 30 percentage points: 60% pain relief with neravixa versus 30% with duloxetine, equivalent to 30 additional patients achieving relief per 100 treated. The sample size will be chosen to give 90% power under these assumptions. Choosing the target requires a judgment about what difference is plausible and important to detect; the uncertain pilot estimate is one source of evidence [@cook2018delta2; @cook2019delta2].

The [clinical threshold](#clinical-threshold) is the smallest additional benefit judged worthwhile. For this teaching case, suppose neravixa requires four additional safety-monitoring visits and carries a risk of short-lived dizziness. Patient and clinical advisers judge that at least 20 additional patients achieving pain relief per 100 treated would justify this additional burden and potential harm compared with duloxetine. This gives a clinical threshold of 20 percentage points. The judgment needs to reflect the particular treatments and patients [@cook2018delta2].

<details class="misconception" id="model-answer-pilot-threshold">
<summary>Common misconception: the minimum clinically worthwhile benefit should equal the difference observed in a pilot</summary>

If the pilot had shown relief in 6 rather than 7 treated patients, should the clinical threshold change?

The observed difference would fall from 40 to 30 percentage points, with standard-treatment relief still at 30%. That changes the evidence about the likely benefit. The clinical threshold remains 20 points because the judgment about worthwhile relief, harms and burden has not changed.

</details>

These values serve different purposes and may coincide or follow a different numerical order in another study. They describe comparisons between groups. The section [Between-group differences and individual benefit](#between-group-differences) explains why they cannot describe the benefit for each individual patient.

| Quantity | Value | Role in this study |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Difference observed in the pilot | 40 percentage points: 70% versus 30% | Sample result that informs planning, with uncertainty |
| Target between-group difference | 30 percentage points: 60% versus 30% | Population difference at which the calculation evaluates power |
| Clinically worthwhile between-group difference (clinical threshold) | 20 percentage points | Smallest additional benefit judged worthwhile, considering burdens, risks, and alternatives |

Table: (\#tab:pain-planning-values) Earlier observations and two planning decisions for the neuropathic pain trial; their numerical values can coincide.

Figure \@ref(fig:planning-differences) places these values on the same scale. All are absolute differences in percentage points. The clinical meaning becomes clearer when a difference is expressed as additional patients benefiting per 100 treated and considered alongside treatment burden. Labels such as “small,” “medium” and “large” need that clinical context [@caldwell2020].

The section [Choosing plausible assumptions](#st01-expectations) discusses how previous findings, target differences, and clinical judgments inform a sample size calculation report.

```{r planning-differences, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=3, fig.cap="Difference observed in the pilot, target difference and clinical threshold for the neuropathic pain trial. The pilot value is a sample result; the target and threshold concern population differences. All are expressed in percentage points. Their values may coincide or follow a different order in other studies.", fig.alt="Three compact horizontal rows share an axis for novel minus standard treatment. Each line starts at zero and ends at its labeled value: difference observed in the pilot, 40 percentage points, calculated from the pilot patients; target difference, 30 points, used to evaluate power; clinical threshold, 20 points, the smallest benefit judged worthwhile."}
draw_planning_differences()
```

The sample size is chosen to give 90% power at the 30-point target difference. If the true benefit is 20 additional patients achieving relief per 100 treated, this trial will detect a difference less often than if the benefit is 30 per 100. The smaller benefit would still be clinically worthwhile. A larger sample is needed to achieve 90% power for that smaller difference. The next section explains power and the two error probabilities.



```{r consider-pilot-target, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_consider_check("consider-pilot-target")
```

## Hypotheses, error probabilities, and power {#power .core-heading}

<span id="hypotheses-and-error-probabilities"></span>

The [null hypothesis](#null-hypothesis) claims that the population pain-relief percentages are equal. The [alternative hypothesis](#alternative-hypothesis) allows a difference in either direction. A statistically significant result provides evidence against the null hypothesis under the test's assumptions.

A [two-sided test](#two-sided-test), also called a two-tailed test, considers whether the novel treatment produces more or less relief than the comparator. It is the usual starting point for a superiority comparison when differences in either direction matter: the new treatment could perform better or worse. This tutorial uses a two-sided Type I error probability of 5%, allowing 2.5% in each tail. A one-sided test requires a scientific justification specified before seeing the results, as ICH E9 explains in section 5.5 [@iche91998].

Let $\delta$ (delta) denote the population difference: neravixa minus duloxetine. Positive values favor neravixa and negative values favor duloxetine. The two-sided test compares:

\begin{equation}
H_0: \delta=0, \qquad H_1: \delta\ne0.
(\#eq:hypotheses)
\end{equation}

A test's decision can agree or disagree with reality: the population pain-relief percentages are either equal or different. Table \@ref(tab:error-table) shows the four possibilities for the neuropathic pain trial.

```{r error-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `Population or decision` = c("Population relief percentages: duloxetine and neravixa", "Correct decision", "Error"),
  `Scenario 1: H0 is true` = c("30% and 30% (equal population relief percentages)", "True negative: do not reject the null", "False positive (Type I error): reject the null"),
  `Scenario 2: H0 is not true` = c("30% and 60% (different population relief percentages)", "True positive (power): reject the null", "False negative (Type II error): do not reject the null"),
  check.names = FALSE), caption = "Two population scenarios and their possible testing decisions in the neuropathic pain trial. Correct decisions precede errors in each scenario.")
```

### Scenario 1: H₀ is true (equal population relief percentages) {#scenario-1-equal-population-relief-percentages .unnumbered}

Suppose both treatments provide relief to 30% of patients. With a 5% Type I error probability, about 95 of every 100 repetitions would correctly leave the null hypothesis unrejected: true negatives. About 5 would incorrectly find a statistically significant difference: false positives.

```{r error-scenario-null, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Equal population relief percentages: 30% with each treatment. The grid illustrates expected frequencies under a 5% Type I error probability. The first 95 blue circles represent true negatives, followed by five amber crosses for false positives. Each tile represents one complete trial.", fig.alt="Red stick figures represent the eligible population with neuropathic pain. Stick figures illustrate 30% relief with each treatment. A 10 by 10 grid begins with 95 blue circles for true negatives, followed by five amber crosses for false positives."}
draw_error_scenario("null")
```

### Scenario 2: H₀ is not true (different population relief percentages) {#scenario-2-different-population-relief-percentages .unnumbered}

Suppose 30% achieve relief with duloxetine and 60% with neravixa. A trial with 90% power at this difference would detect a statistically significant difference in about 90 of every 100 repetitions: true positives. About 10 would fail to detect it: false negatives.

```{r error-scenario-effect, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Different population relief percentages: 30% with standard treatment and 60% with novel treatment. The grid illustrates expected frequencies for trials designed for 90% power at this difference. The first 90 blue circles represent true positives, followed by ten amber crosses for false negatives. Each tile represents one complete trial.", fig.alt="Red stick figures represent the eligible population with neuropathic pain. Stick figures illustrate 30% relief with duloxetine and 60% with neravixa. A 10 by 10 grid begins with 90 blue circles for true positives, followed by ten amber crosses for false negatives."}
draw_error_scenario("effect")
```


```{r consider-false-negative, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_consider_check("consider-false-negative")
```

Scenario 1 (equal population relief percentages) and Scenario 2 (different population relief percentages) give the error probabilities their meaning:

- [Type I error probability](#alpha), written $\alpha$ (alpha), is the probability of falsely rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true: a [false positive](#false-positive).
- [Type II error probability](#beta), written $\beta$ (beta), is the probability of failing to reject the null hypothesis at a specified true difference: a [false negative](#false-negative).
- [Power](#statistical-power) is the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis at that specified true difference: a true positive. It equals $1-\beta$, so 90% power corresponds to a 10% Type II error probability.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-power-meaning">
<summary>Common misconception: 90% power means a 90% probability that the treatment works</summary>

Suppose the population relief percentages really are 60% with neravixa and 30% with duloxetine. A design with 90% power would detect a difference in about 900 of 1,000 trials conducted under those assumptions. As more trials are added, the detected fraction tends toward the test's power, with smaller random fluctuations. This calculation assumes the population difference when evaluating the test.

</details>

A false positive could contribute to adopting a treatment that adds burden without improving pain relief. A false negative could delay recognition of a worthwhile benefit. These consequences, alongside methodological and regulatory guidance, inform the chosen error probabilities. The neuropathic pain plan uses a two-sided Type I error probability of 5% and 90% power at the 30-point target difference.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-Type I error probability-meaning">
<summary>Common misconception: a significant result has only a 5% probability of being a false positive</summary>

The 5% refers to trials where the population relief percentages are equal. In 1,000 such trials, a test with a 5% false-positive probability would give about 50 significant results. To ask how many significant findings are false positives also requires information about how often treatments truly differ and how much power the studies have.

</details>

The trial itself is conducted once. Calculations and repeated simulations help assess how often its planned test would detect a difference under specified population assumptions. The sample size calculation evaluates power at the 30-point target difference. The test evaluates evidence against a population difference of zero.



## One trial and repeated trials {#activity-1-one-study-then-many .core-heading}

The pilot observed 70% versus 30% relief. In the [simulation](#statistical-simulation), the computer generates possible trial outcomes using the planning assumptions of 60% relief with neravixa and 30% with duloxetine. The population difference is known, so each trial estimate can be compared with it.

### Three trials under the same assumptions {#a-couple-of-individual-trials .core-heading}

The computer generates three trials with 20 patients per group and calculates their observed relief differences. Each trial has different patient outcomes under the same population assumptions. Figure \@ref(fig:three-pain-trials) follows each trial from its patient outcomes to its estimated treatment difference.

```{r pain-sample-estimates}
# <- saves a result under a name. lapply() repeats the same steps for each trial.
# The population probabilities stay fixed; each run generates new patients.
example_trials <- lapply(20260941:20260943, function(trial_seed) {
  scenario <- study_spec(outcome = "proportions", n = 20,
    p_control = .30, p_treatment = .60, threshold = .20,
    seed = trial_seed)
  simulate_one_study(scenario)
})
# Combine one row per trial into a table. [[i]] selects trial i from the list.
trial_examples <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(example_trials), function(i) {
  trial <- example_trials[[i]]
  # For 0/1 outcomes, the mean within each group is its observed relief fraction.
  rates <- tapply(trial$data$outcome, trial$data$group, mean)
  data.frame(Trial = i, `duloxetine: achieved pain relief` = percent(rates["Control"]),
    `neravixa: achieved pain relief` = percent(rates["Treatment"]),
    `Observed difference` = paste0(round(100 * trial$result$estimate), " percentage points"),
    check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
}))
# kable() formats the results as a readable table.
knitr::kable(trial_examples, caption = "Three simulated trials with 20 patients per group, all sampled under the same 30% and 60% population event probabilities.")
```

```{r three-pain-trials, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=6.5, fig.cap="Three simulated trials with 20 patients per group. All use the same population pain-relief probabilities: 30% with duloxetine and 60% with neravixa. Green stick figures show achieved pain relief and red figures show no pain relief. Arrows connect each pair of groups to its observed difference. The dashed green line marks the population difference of 30 percentage points. The blue line marks the mean of the three trial estimates.", fig.alt="Three rows show individual patient outcomes in the duloxetine and neravixa groups, their relief counts and percentages, and the resulting treatment differences on a shared scale. The eligible population and sampled outcomes use stick figures. Patient outcomes and estimates vary while the population difference stays at 30 percentage points. A blue line marks the mean of the three estimates."}
draw_three_pain_trials(example_trials)
```

These trials share population probabilities, group sizes, allocation and testing procedure. Their patient outcomes, observed percentages, differences and decisions vary. The simulation makes the distinction between population and sample visible because its population parameters are known.


```{r consider-sampling, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_consider_check("consider-sampling")
```

### Many trials and a larger sample {.core-heading}

Repeating the trial 5,000 times shows a range of possible sample differences. As a rule, larger samples produce less variable estimates. The 5,000 estimates from larger samples form a tighter cluster around the population difference. Separately, as more simulated trials are added at any fixed sample size, their average difference tends toward the known 30-point population difference. More repetitions make the simulation summary more stable.

```{r three-samples}
# c() collects the three patient counts to compare.
sample_sizes <- c(20, 50, 80)
# Repeat 5,000 trials at each count; n is patients per group, B is trials.
batches <- lapply(sample_sizes, function(n) {
  scenario <- study_spec(outcome = "proportions", n = n,
    p_control = .30, p_treatment = .60, threshold = .20,
    width_target = .20, B = 5000, seed = 20260921 + n)
  simulate_trials(scenario)
})
# Extract and combine each batch's percentage of significant results.
power_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(batches, power_row))
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Patients per group` = power_results$n_per_group,
  `Estimated power` = percent(power_results$simulated_power),
  check.names = FALSE), caption = "Estimated power: the percentage of 5,000 simulated trials detecting the true 30-percentage-point relief difference at each sample size.")
```

```{r sample-differences, echo=FALSE, fig.height=9, fig.cap="Observed treatment differences across 5,000 simulated trials at each sample size. The dashed line marks the specified population difference of 30 percentage points. As a rule, larger samples produce less variable estimates.", fig.alt="Three histograms of observed relief differences with 20, 50 and 80 patients per group, showing progressively narrower distributions around the same population difference of 30 percentage points."}
local({
  old_par <- par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(5.4, 4, 3.7, 1))
  on.exit(par(old_par))
  for (batch in batches) {
    hist(100 * batch$results$estimate, breaks = seq(-100, 100, 5),
      xlim = c(-40, 90), col = "#b9d4f3", border = "white",
      main = paste(batch$spec$n, "patients per group"),
      xlab = "", ylab = "Number of trials")
    abline(v = 30, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "#69509a")
    axis(1, at = 30, labels = FALSE, col.ticks = "#69509a")
    mtext("30 percentage points: true population difference", side = 1, at = 30, line = 2.2, cex = .8, col = "#69509a")
    mtext("Observed difference in relief (percentage points)", side = 1, line = 4, cex = .8)
  }
})
```

Figure \@ref(fig:sample-differences) shows [sampling variability](#sampling-variability). Table \@ref(tab:three-samples) estimates power by counting statistically significant results when the true difference is 30 percentage points. With equal population relief percentages, the percentage of significant results would instead estimate the Type I error probability. The assumed true difference here equals the 30-point [target difference](#target-difference) used to evaluate power. The simulation uses the specified population probabilities of 30% and 60%.

<span id="model-answer-sample-versus-population"></span>

Increasing the sample size changes the information in each trial. Increasing simulation repetitions makes the estimated percentage of significant results more stable; each trial retains the same sample size and power.

The app below starts with 20 patients per group. In Scenario 1, $H_0$ is true: both treatments provide 30% population relief. In Scenario 2, $H_0$ is not true: population relief is 30% with duloxetine and 60% with neravixa. Each trial contributes patient outcomes, an estimated difference, a two-sided p value and a test decision [@superpowerbook2022; @thiesmeier2024; @rudolph2021].

Step 4 plots the two-sided p values. A sufficiently large positive or negative difference produces a small p value. Values below 0.05 reject the hypothesis of equal population relief percentages. Steps 2–3 show the direction of the observed difference. The 100-tile grid summarizes the decision percentages across all completed trials, rounded to whole percentages. Exact counts appear above it.

In Scenario 1 ($H_0$ is true), the p values have spikes and gaps because relief counts are whole numbers. Equal counts, such as 6 of 20 patients in each group, give p = 1. At these population settings, equal counts occur in about 14 of every 100 trials. Increasing the number of simulated trials makes this pattern clearer. Increasing the patients per group allows a finer range of p values.

```{r pain-app-preview, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_app_preview("pain_one_many", "Simulate further trials and compare different sample sizes.",
  image = "../figures/pain-trials-preview.png")
```

<div class="chapter-recap">

### Take-home points {.unnumbered}

- A sample size calculation starts with the research question and planned analysis.
- A pilot result describes its sample; relevant evidence and uncertainty inform the main study assumptions.
- Power is the probability of rejecting the null under a specified true difference.
- Comparing sample sizes under the same population assumptions shows how additional patients affect sampling variability and power. More simulation repetitions make the summaries more stable.
- The target difference and clinical threshold have distinct roles and may have the same value.

</div>

# Calculating sample size and recruitment {#calculations .core-heading}


::: {.learning-goals .core-outcomes}
After this chapter, you should be able to:

- Compare calculations after changing one input to explain how the [target difference](#target-difference), [event probabilities](#event-probability) or [standard deviation](#standard-deviation), [Type I error probability](#alpha), and target [power](#statistical-power) affect sample size.
- Calculate the [analyzable sample size](#analyzable-sample-size) for two independent proportions or means.
- Interpret per-group and total counts, including upward rounding.
- Identify the procedure and inputs needed to reproduce a calculation.
- Calculate a recruitment target allowing for expected missing outcomes.
- Assess recruitment feasibility using a screening and enrollment funnel.

:::

The neuropathic pain trial now has a defined comparison: neravixa versus duloxetine, with pain relief assessed at four weeks. The plan uses 60% versus 30% relief, a target difference of 30 percentage points, a 5% Type I error probability and 90% power. How many patients would provide enough outcomes for this comparison, and how many should the clinics recruit?

This chapter turns those assumptions into patient counts. It first calculates the required analyzable sample, then allows for missing outcomes and checks recruitment time. A continuous-outcome example shows how the calculation changes when the outcome is a score. Both comparisons assume two [independent groups](#independent-groups), equal allocation and a [two-sided test](#two-sided-test). The section [Units of randomization, measurement, and analysis](#units-of-analysis) covers paired and clustered designs.

## How error probabilities and power affect sample size {#how-error-rates-and-power-affect-sample-size .core-heading}

For the neuropathic pain trial, a 5% Type I error probability means that, if the treatments were equally effective, about 5 in 100 repeated trials would falsely conclude that they differ. Choosing 1% would reduce that allowance to about 1 in 100. The stronger evidence required would also increase the sample size.

The 90% power target concerns a different scenario: if relief occurs in 60% with neravixa and 30% with duloxetine, about 90 in 100 trials should detect a difference. Raising the target to 95 in 100 would require more patients. These choices determine how much evidence the trial must provide at the selected 30-point difference.

For the normal approximation, these choices are translated into [$z$-values](#z-value): positions on the standard normal bell-shaped curve, centered at zero with a standard deviation of one. The sample size formulas use one value for the Type I error probability, $z_{1-\alpha/2}$, and another for target power, $z_{1-\beta}$.

Here, $\alpha$ (alpha) is the Type I error probability, $\beta$ (beta) is the [Type II error probability](#beta), and $1-\beta$ is the target power.

A $z$-value describes how many standard deviations a position lies from the center of that curve. Its subscript gives the proportion of the distribution below that position. For example, $z_{0.975}=1.96$ means that 97.5% of the distribution lies below 1.96. This position is called a [quantile](#quantile).

For a two-sided Type I error probability of 5% and target power of 90%:

- The 5% error allowance is split between the two ends of the distribution: 2.5% in each tail. This gives $z_{1-0.05/2}=z_{0.975}\approx1.96$.
- The target power of 90% gives $z_{0.90}\approx1.28$.

Figure \@ref(fig:normal-multiplier) shows what these distances mean for a treatment comparison. The upper curve applies when the population difference is zero; the lower applies when it equals the target difference. The same rejection boundaries apply in both cases. Separating the centers by about 1.96 + 1.28 standard errors puts about 90% of the lower curve beyond the upper boundary.

The formulas below combine these two $z$-values with the target difference and outcome variability. A lower Type I error probability increases the first $z$-value, and higher target power increases the second. Either change requires more patients when the other inputs stay the same [@kirkwood2003; @wang2020].

```{r normal-multiplier, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=6, fig.cap="The two curves represent different population scenarios. Above: no treatment difference (H0 true), with 5% in the two rejection tails. Below: the target difference (H0 false), with approximately 90% beyond the upper rejection boundary. The centers are separated by 1.96 + 1.28 = 3.24 standard errors.", fig.alt="Two sampling distributions on the same standard-error scale. The upper distribution is centered at zero under H0; the lower is centered at the target difference, 3.24 standard errors above zero. The same rejection boundaries are used for both. Shading shows false positives under H0 and power at the target difference."}
draw_normal_cutoffs()
```

## Two proportions {.core-heading}

The event percentages in each group and the target difference between them are your starting inputs. For the neuropathic pain trial, the calculation assumes 60% relief with the novel treatment and 30% with standard treatment: a target difference of 30 [percentage points](#percentage-points).

For two independent groups of equal size, the normal approximation uses the two $z$-values illustrated in Figure \@ref(fig:normal-multiplier). Each is multiplied by the variability for its scenario before the terms are added and squared. Let $p_t$ and $p_c$ be the novel- and standard-treatment relief probabilities, and let $\bar p=(p_t+p_c)/2$ be their average. The required number in each group is approximately:

\begin{equation}
n\approx\frac{\left[z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{2\bar p(1-\bar p)}+
z_{1-\beta}\sqrt{p_t(1-p_t)+p_c(1-p_c)}\right]^2}{(p_t-p_c)^2}.
(\#eq:proportions-normal)
\end{equation}

The quantities under the square roots describe variability in the two scenarios: equal treatment probabilities for the test boundary, and the specified treatment probabilities for power. The denominator is the squared target difference. With $p_t=0.60$, $p_c=0.30$, and $\bar p=0.45$:

\begin{equation}
n\approx\frac{\left[1.96\sqrt{2\times0.45\times0.55}+
1.282\sqrt{0.60\times0.40+0.30\times0.70}\right]^2}{(0.60-0.30)^2}
\approx55.7.
(\#eq:proportions-worked)
\end{equation}

R's `power.prop.test()` uses unrounded cutoffs and includes both rejection tails with `strict = TRUE` [@rcore]. Rounding its result upward gives 56 analyzable patients per group, or 112 in total.

```{r multiplier-table, echo=FALSE}
# Keep relief probabilities fixed while comparing error and power choices.
grid <- expand.grid(alpha = c(.05, .01), power = c(.80, .90, .95))
grid$per_group <- mapply(function(a, p) sample_size_two_proportions(.60, .30, a, p),
  grid$alpha, grid$power)
shown <- display_probabilities(grid, c("alpha", "power"))
names(shown)[names(shown) == "per group"] <- "Analyzable patients per group"
knitr::kable(shown, digits = 2,
  caption = "Analyzable patients per group for different Type I error probabilities and target powers, with relief probabilities fixed at 60% and 30%.")
```

Table \@ref(tab:multiplier-table) connects the cutoffs to recruitment planning. At 5% Type I error probability and 90% power, the calculation gives 56 analyzable patients per group. Lowering the error probability to 1% or raising power to 95% increases that requirement, with the relief probabilities unchanged.


```{r consider-smaller-target, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_consider_check("consider-smaller-target")
```

```{r error-power-counts, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="Analyzable patients per group under four error and power choices, with relief probabilities fixed at 60% and 30%. The blue point marks the neuropathic pain plan. Each other row changes one choice.", fig.alt="A horizontal patient-count plot compares the current plan, lower and higher target power, and a lower Type I error probability, keeping the treatment relief probabilities fixed."}
draw_error_power_counts()
```

```{r proportions}
# Relief probabilities for novel treatment (t) and standard treatment (c).
pi_t <- .60
pi_c <- .30
# With n omitted, R finds patients per group for the requested power.
# two.sided allows either direction; strict = TRUE counts both rejection tails.
pain_plan <- power.prop.test(p1 = pi_t, p2 = pi_c,
  sig.level = .05, power = .90,
  alternative = "two.sided", strict = TRUE)
# $n selects the calculated count. ceiling() rounds upward to a whole patient.
n_raw <- pain_plan$n
n_per_group <- ceiling(n_raw)
# Retain this count for the later recruitment example.
pain_lab_n <- n_per_group
c(per_group = n_per_group, total = 2 * n_per_group)
```

```{r proportions-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=n_per_group, `Analyzable total`=2*n_per_group, check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Analyzable sample size for the neuropathic pain trial using the normal planning approximation.")
```

These are patients with an outcome available for analysis. The recruitment allowance is calculated separately below.

The normal approximation targets 90% power under these assumptions. Simulation can examine the performance of the planned test.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-definitive-sample">
<summary>Common misconception: the calculator gives one correct sample size for my research question</summary>

For the neuropathic pain trial, 60% versus 30% relief requires 56 patients per group. Planning for 50% versus 30% requires more patients at the same power and Type I error probability. The result follows from the entered assumptions. The report should identify those assumptions and whether the count is per group or total.

</details>

```{r proportion-changes}
# Each row specifies a different set of assumptions.
proportion_cases <- data.frame(
  scenario = c("Original", "Smaller difference", "Lower probabilities"),
  treatment = c(.60, .60, .30),
  control = c(.30, .45, .15),
  alpha = c(.05, .05, .05),
  power = c(.90, .90, .90))
# mapply() calculates a sample size for each row using its four inputs.
proportion_cases$per_group <- mapply(sample_size_two_proportions,
  proportion_cases$treatment, proportion_cases$control,
  proportion_cases$alpha, proportion_cases$power)
proportion_cases$total <- 2 * proportion_cases$per_group
# Convert probabilities to percentages for display; calculations use decimals.
knitr::kable(display_probabilities(proportion_cases,
  c("treatment", "control", "alpha", "power")),
  caption = "Analyzable sample sizes under alternative binary-outcome assumptions, using the same normal planning approximation as the tutorial and apps.")
```

For a yes/no outcome, the calculation uses the event percentage in each group. For example, 30% versus 15% and 60% versus 45% both differ by 15 percentage points, but they need not require the same sample size. The amount of [sampling variability](#sampling-variability) also depends on where those percentages lie. Halving the difference therefore does not necessarily multiply the required sample size by exactly four. The table lets you compare these assumptions directly.

Read a row as a conditional statement: if those event probabilities and that analysis are reasonable, then this is the approximate number required for the specified error targets. The smaller-difference row needs more participants because sampling variability makes that difference harder to distinguish from zero.

In the [two-proportion app](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/two_proportions/), you can compare the sample sizes needed at different power targets.

<div id="calculate-sample-size">

```{r calculation-app-preview, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_app_preview("pain_calculation", "Calculate the neuropathic pain trial's analyzable requirement, then use the recruitment section below to allow for unavailable outcomes.")
```

</div>

At a 20-percentage-point target difference (50% versus 30%), the same procedure requires `r report_example$facts$sensitivity_n` analyzable patients per group for 90% power, compared with `r report_example$facts$analyzable` at 30 points. This quantifies the decision introduced in Chapter 1: detecting the smaller worthwhile difference with the same power requires more patients.

<details id="adherence" class="optional-practice">
<summary>Additional practice: preventing gestational diabetes</summary>

Suppose you want to find out whether probiotic supplementation prevents gestational diabetes in pregnant women with overweight or obesity (BMI at least 25 kg/m²). Randomly allocate women to probiotics or no probiotics, with otherwise comparable care, and assess gestational diabetes using a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). Your plan should specify the supplement, diagnostic criteria and assessment time before planning. An assessment at 20–24 weeks needs justification against applicable clinical guidance: NICE generally recommends risk-based testing at 24–28 weeks [@nicegdm]. For an observational study of supplementation, confounding requires an appropriate analysis and planning method.

For this calculation, assume gestational diabetes occurs in 20% without probiotics and 10% with probiotics. The target reduction is 10 percentage points. The task is to express the outcome consistently when entering these percentages.

The same planning assumption can be expressed using either developing the disease or remaining free of it:

| Outcome entered | Without probiotics | With probiotics |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Develops gestational diabetes | 20% | 10% |
| Remains free of gestational diabetes | 80% | 90% |

Table: (\#tab:gdm-outcome-direction) Two ways to express the same assumed effect of probiotics.

The [probiotics calculation activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/book/calculations.html#activity-probiotics_calculation) uses the second row. A 10-percentage-point increase in remaining disease-free represents the same comparison as a 10-percentage-point reduction in developing the disease. Your report should identify the event entered.

```{r adherence-case}
# Load the same example inputs used by the app.
adherence_case <- teaching_case("adherence")
adherence_plan <- teaching_case_spec("adherence")
# Calculate patients per group for the example's target power.
adherence_plan$n <- plan_n(adherence_plan, "testing",
  adherence_case$inputs$target_power)
# Display the analyzable count in each group and across both groups.
c(analyzable_per_group = adherence_plan$n,
  analyzable_total = 2 * adherence_plan$n,
  planning_power = spec_power(adherence_plan))
```

  caption = "Analyzable sample size for the hypothetical gestational-diabetes prevention trial.")
```

## Two means {.core-heading}

For a continuous outcome, you should identify the target difference and the [standard deviation](#standard-deviation) in the same measurement units before calculating.

In the formula below, $n$ is the number of patients needed in each group, $\delta$ (delta) is the target difference between the group means, and $\sigma$ (sigma) is the assumed SD of individual scores within each group. The calculation assumes the same SD in both groups. The two $z$-values introduced above are added and squared. The factor $2\sigma^2$ accounts for variability in both independent groups:

\begin{equation}
n\approx\frac{2\sigma^2\left(z_{1-\alpha/2}+z_{1-\beta}\right)^2}{\delta^2}.
(\#eq:means)
\end{equation}

Suppose an earlier study observed a 4-unit [between-group difference](#expected-difference) in a normally distributed improvement score. The calculation uses a target difference of 3 units and an SD of 5 units in both groups. Patients and clinicians judge a 2-unit benefit clinically important. The example uses a hypothetical, approximately normally distributed improvement score. The Type I error probability is 5% and target power is 90%.

The normal formula makes the calculation transparent:

\begin{equation}
n\approx\frac{2\times5^2\times(1.96+1.282)^2}{3^2}\approx58.4.
(\#eq:means-worked)
\end{equation}

```{r means}
# Target mean difference and common standard deviation, in score units.
delta <- 3
sigma <- 5
# Probabilities are entered as decimals: .05 = 5%, .90 = 90%.
alpha <- .05
target_power <- .90
# qnorm() gives each normal cutoff. Divide alpha by 2 for a two-sided test.
z_error <- qnorm(1 - alpha / 2)
z_power <- qnorm(target_power)
# The normal formula illustrates how the inputs affect the requirement.
# The factor 2 allows for variability in both independent groups.
normal_n_raw <- 2 * sigma^2 * (z_error + z_power)^2 / delta^2
c(unrounded_per_group = normal_n_raw,
  rounded_per_group = ceiling(normal_n_raw))
```

The normal approximation gives 58.4 patients per group, which rounds upward to 59. The planned analysis is a pooled two-sample t-test, which accounts for estimating the common SD from the trial data. Its sample size calculation gives 60 patients per group. The trial would therefore need outcomes from 60 patients in each group, or 120 altogether, for 90% power at a three-point mean difference with SD five.

```{r t-test-planning}
# Plan the pooled two-sample t test with the same inputs.
# strict = TRUE includes rejection in either direction.
t_plan <- power.t.test(delta = delta, sd = sigma, sig.level = alpha,
  power = target_power, type = "two.sample", alternative = "two.sided",
  strict = TRUE)
# Round upward within each group, then add the two groups.
n_per_group <- ceiling(t_plan$n)
t_plan
c(per_group = n_per_group, total = 2 * n_per_group)
```

```{r means-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=n_per_group, `Analyzable total`=2*n_per_group, check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Analyzable sample size for the continuous-outcome comparison, planned for a pooled two-sample t test.")
```

Smaller target differences require larger samples because they are harder to distinguish from patient-to-patient variation. In the normal formula, halving the difference or doubling the SD multiplies the unrounded requirement by four. The t-test calculation gives approximately this increase.


```{r consider-halve-difference, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_consider_check("consider-halve-difference")
```

<details>
<summary>Raw and standardized differences</summary>

The target difference of 3 score units is a raw between-group difference. Dividing it by the common SD gives the standardized difference: $d=3/5=0.60$. If the SD were 10 units, the same 3-unit difference would give $d=0.30$. The clinical difference is unchanged, but it is smaller relative to patient-to-patient variation and requires more patients to detect. A standardized effect is therefore not, by itself, a measure of clinical importance. Keeping the difference in the outcome's original units helps you explain what it would mean clinically; standardized measures can help compare results across scales [@kallogjeri2023].

</details>

<details>
<summary>Where does the assumed SD come from?</summary>

Previous studies can inform the assumed SD. The most relevant evidence uses similar patients, the same outcome scale and assessment time, and a compatible analysis. For an analysis of change scores, the required SD describes changes within patients. For an analysis of final scores, it describes those final scores. Reviews show that variability can differ substantially between studies, supporting examination of a plausible range [@bentin2026].

Your sample size calculation report should document the source of the assumed SD and examine a plausible range using the [two-means app](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/two_means/).

</details>

Your sample size calculation report should record the inputs, pooled two-sample t-test procedure, software, two-sided test, equal allocation, and rounded counts. The [software and statistical support guide](#software-support) reviews calculation software and explains when early advice from a statistician is useful. Its [worked example](#gpower-assumptions) shows how an effect-size input can change the result.

<details id="rehabilitation" class="optional-practice">
<summary>Additional practice: rehabilitation</summary>

For additional practice, consider six-week mobility improvement in two independent rehabilitation groups. The calculation above used a target difference of 3 score units and a common SD of 5. How would the required sample change if relevant evidence instead supported an SD of 7, with the other inputs unchanged?

```{r rehabilitation-case}
# Load the rehabilitation example shared with the app.
rehabilitation_case <- teaching_case("rehabilitation")
rehabilitation_plan <- teaching_case_spec("rehabilitation")
# Calculate patients per group from the difference, SD, error probability and power.
rehabilitation_plan$n <- sample_size_two_means(
  rehabilitation_case$inputs$plan_delta, rehabilitation_case$inputs$plan_sd,
  rehabilitation_case$inputs$alpha, rehabilitation_case$inputs$target_power)
# Report the analyzable requirement before the recruitment adjustment in Chapter 2.
c(analyzable_per_group = rehabilitation_plan$n,
  total = 2 * rehabilitation_plan$n)
```

```{r rehabilitation-case-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=rehabilitation_plan$n, `Analyzable total`=2*rehabilitation_plan$n, check.names=FALSE), caption="Analyzable sample size for the rehabilitation comparison.")
```

<details id="rehabilitation-report">
<summary>Example report for the mean-score comparison</summary>

<div class="annotated-report" role="group" aria-label="Sample size calculation report for the rehabilitation trial">

<p class="report-part">Question and design</p>

<span class="report-mark">Question and outcome:</span> The trial compares mean improvement in mobility scores six weeks after starting the novel or standard rehabilitation program. <span class="report-mark">Allocation and analysis unit:</span> Participants are individually randomized 1:1, with one improvement score per participant and independent treatment groups.

<p class="report-part">Assumptions and evidence</p>

<span class="report-mark">Target difference and variability:</span> The calculation uses a 3-unit difference and a common SD of 5 units, corresponding to a standardized difference of 0.60. The report should identify the clinical basis for three units and the studies supporting the SD on this outcome scale. <span class="report-mark">Sensitivity analysis:</span> An SD of 7 would increase the requirement to `r sample_size_two_means(3, 7, .05, .90)` patients per group, with the other inputs unchanged.

<p class="report-part">Calculation</p>

<span class="report-mark">Procedure:</span> A two-sided pooled two-sample t test, with a 5% Type I error probability and 90% target power at a 3-unit difference. <span class="report-mark">Software:</span> R `r report_example$r_version`, stats `r report_example$stats_version`, and `power.t.test(delta=3, sd=5, sig.level=.05, power=.90, type="two.sample", alternative="two.sided", strict=TRUE)`. <span class="report-mark">Required sample:</span> Rounding upward gives `r rehabilitation_plan$n` analyzable patients per group, or `r 2*rehabilitation_plan$n` in total.

<p class="report-part">Recruitment and conclusion</p>

<span class="report-mark">Recruitment:</span> Allowing for 5% unavailable six-week outcomes gives `r ceiling(rehabilitation_plan$n/.95)` recruits per group (`r 2*ceiling(rehabilitation_plan$n/.95)` total). The loss assumption and recruitment period should be supported by follow-up and screening records. <span class="report-mark">Intended conclusion:</span> The trial evaluates whether mean improvement differs between the programs. The observed difference and its uncertainty will inform its clinical interpretation.

</div>

</details>

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-rehabilitation-sd">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The pooled t-test calculation increases from `r rehabilitation_plan$n` to `r sample_size_two_means(3, 7, .05, .90)` analyzable patients per group. The larger SD represents more variation between patients, so more observations are needed to distinguish the same 3-unit difference. The evidence supporting the selected SD belongs in the report.

</details>

Although an improvement score uses before/after information within each patient, this example analyzes one score per patient across two independent groups. A single-group paired comparison, repeated-measures model, or baseline-adjusted analysis needs its own planning method.

<details class="advanced-explanation">
<summary>Simulate rehabilitation outcomes</summary>

The [rehabilitation simulation](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/power_explorer/?activity=rehabilitation) uses a t-test planning method. *One trial* generates independent, normally distributed improvement scores. Its test evaluates evidence against a zero population difference. *Repeated trials* shows how conclusions vary under the same population assumptions. This extension can be used after the core calculation.

</details>

```{r rehabilitation-app-preview, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_app_preview("rehabilitation_calculation", "Compare SDs of 5 and 7 for a target difference of 3 units on the same graph, then justify the scenario selected for your report.")
```

</details>

The [discharge exercise](#discharge) offers additional practice with a binary outcome.

<span id="feasibility"></span>

## Allowing for expected missing outcomes {#account-for-expected-losses .core-heading}

The neuropathic pain trial needs 56 usable outcomes per group. If 5% of recruited patients are expected to have no four-week outcome, the clinics need to recruit more than 56 per group. Here, $n$ is the required number per group and $r$ is the expected proportion lost, so $1-r$ is the expected [retention proportion](#retention). The brackets mean "round upward to the next whole patient":

\begin{equation}
n_{\mathrm{recruit,arm}}=\left\lceil\frac{n}{1-r}\right\rceil.
(\#eq:dropout)
\end{equation}

For 56 analyzable patients per group and 5% expected loss, $r=0.05$ and the expected retained fraction is $1-0.05=0.95$:

\begin{equation}
n_{\mathrm{recruit,arm}}=\left\lceil\frac{56}{1-0.05}\right\rceil
=\left\lceil58.95\right\rceil=59.
(\#eq:dropout-worked)
\end{equation}

The clinics would therefore recruit 59 patients for each treatment, or 118 altogether, to aim for 112 usable outcomes.

The expected loss should draw on studies or records with a comparable population, treatment, outcome and follow-up period. For example, if 10 of 200 enrolled patients in a comparable study lacked the required outcome, the observed loss was 10/200 = 5%. Using $r=0.05$ in the new trial assumes that this experience is relevant. Reasons for missing outcomes, differences between arms and uncertainty in a small pilot should inform that judgment. When evidence is limited, your report should identify a plausible range and show how recruitment changes across it.

```{r recruitment}
# Start with the 56 patients per group needed for analysis.
analyzable_per_group <- pain_lab_n
# Divide by the expected retained fraction, 95%, then round upward.
recruit_per_group <- ceiling(analyzable_per_group / (1 - .05))
c(analyzable_per_group = analyzable_per_group,
  recruit_per_group = recruit_per_group, recruit_total = 2 * recruit_per_group)
```

```{r recruitment-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=analyzable_per_group, `Recruit per group`=recruit_per_group, `Recruit total`=2*recruit_per_group, check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Neuropathic pain recruitment target allowing for 5% expected loss.")
```

```{r recruitment-counts, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=3.3, fig.cap="The neuropathic pain calculation gives 56 analyzable patients per group. Dividing by 0.95 and rounding upward within each group gives a recruitment target of 59 per group. The totals include both treatment groups.", fig.alt="Two connected boxes show 56 analyzable patients per group, 112 total, followed by division by 0.95 and upward rounding to 59 recruits per group, 118 total."}
draw_recruitment_counts(analyzable_per_group, .05)
```

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-dropout-arithmetic">
<summary>Common misconception: 10% expected dropout is covered by adding 10% to the required analyzable sample</summary>

If you expect 10% of participants to be lost, approximately 90% will remain. You should therefore divide the required analyzable sample size by 0.90. For example, 100 analyzable participants require recruiting 112 participants after rounding up.

</details>

<span id="model-answer-protocol-counts"></span>
The protocol should report both the required [analyzable sample](#analyzable-sample-size) and the recruitment target, per group and in total: here, `r 2 * analyzable_per_group` analyzable patients and `r 2 * recruit_per_group` recruits across the two groups.

Missing outcomes may be more common in one treatment group or among patients with poor outcomes. Your study should plan for follow-up and an appropriate analysis as well as the expected count. The [missing-outcome extension](#explore-missing-outcomes) examines unequal losses and possible bias.


```{r recruitment-app-preview, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_app_preview("recruitment", "Use your analyzable count and one expected loss percentage to calculate recruitment per group and in total.")
```



```{r consider-recruitment, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_consider_check("consider-recruitment")
```

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-dropout">
<summary>Common misconception: recruiting extra patients removes bias caused by missing outcomes</summary>

Suppose patients with persistent pain are more likely to miss follow-up. The observed relief percentage may then be too high, even after extra patients are recruited. Preventing missing outcomes and choosing an appropriate analysis address this problem [@little2012missing].

</details>

Treatment discontinuation, switching and rescue medication can affect the treatment difference used in planning. The section [Treatment changes and the outcome you want to compare](#treatment-changes) explains how these events enter the research question and calculation.

## Assessing recruitment feasibility {#recruitment-feasibility .core-heading}

The recruitment target should be compared with the number of patients the clinics can enroll within the available time. Screening records help distinguish patients seen in routine care from those who meet the study criteria, can participate and agree to enroll.

For example, the clinics see 100 potentially relevant patients each month. Of these, 40 are eligible and 30 remain available after allowing for competing studies and practical barriers. If half of those 30 consent, expected recruitment is 15 participants per month. Each step uses the patients remaining after the previous step.

```{r recruitment-funnel, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.8, fig.cap="Monthly recruitment funnel for the neuropathic pain trial. Each stage is conditional on the preceding stage: 100 potentially relevant patients, 40 eligible, 30 available, and 15 enrolled. Counts refer to distinct patients.", fig.alt="A narrowing funnel shows 100 potentially relevant patients per month, then 40 meeting eligibility criteria, 30 available after competing studies and practical barriers, and 15 consenting and enrolling. Half of the 30 available patients consent."}
draw_recruitment_funnel()
```

At this rate, recruiting `r 2 * recruit_per_group` patients would take `r ceiling(2 * recruit_per_group / 15)` whole months. The report should also consider site-opening delays and a slower recruitment scenario. The section [Choosing plausible assumptions](#st01-expectations) examines the evidence behind recruitment forecasts, while [Options when the study provides insufficient information](#what-if-the-study-is-too-small-for-its-purpose) discusses changes to the design or recruitment plan.

<span id="lasagnas-law"></span>

*Lasagna's law* describes overestimating how many patients are available for a study. In the screening funnel, 100 potentially relevant patients per month becomes 15 recruits after eligibility, competing demands and consent are considered. Recent screening records should support the recruitment forecast [@lasagna1979].
```{r consider-recruitment-time, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_consider_check("consider-recruitment-time")
```



<div class="chapter-recap">

### Take-home points {.unnumbered}

- Two-group calculations depend on the target difference, variability or event probabilities, Type I error probability and power.
- Comparing one changed assumption with the original plan helps explain its effect. The selected result should identify analyzable participants per group and in total.
- Recruitment allows for expected missing outcomes, with rounding upward within each group.
- Screening and enrollment records help assess whether the recruitment target is feasible.

</div>

<span id="check-feasibility"></span>

# The sample size calculation report {#reporting .core-heading}

::: {.learning-goals .core-outcomes}
After this chapter, you should be able to:

- Identify the essential elements in a worked sample size calculation report.
- Evaluate whether its assumptions, analysis and participant counts agree.
- Correct incomplete or inconsistent reporting.
- Write a concise calculation report with traceable inputs, software and supporting reasoning.
:::

The neuropathic pain calculation gives 56 analyzable patients and 59 recruits per group. A reader should be able to reproduce those numbers and understand why the inputs were chosen. This chapter brings that reasoning and the calculation together in a report. The [report activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/assumptions_report/?stage=question) combines the research question, evidence, assumptions, calculation and recruitment justification in one sample size calculation report.

## A worked sample size calculation report {#write-a-sample-size-justification .core-heading}

Example 3.1 shows the report produced when the neuropathic pain teaching example is selected in the [report activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/assumptions_report/?stage=review). Its four parts bring together the decisions developed in Chapters 1 and 2. The blue labels identify the entries that can be edited in the activity.

The example and checklist follow PICO, SPIRIT 2025, CONSORT 2025, DELTA² and section 4.1 of the UMCG SAP template [@richardson1995; @spiritconsort2025; @consortee2025; @cook2018delta2; @umcgsap; @roa2024comet]. UMCG students and researchers can access the [SAP template in Zenya](https://umcg.zenya.work/document/2f52710d-3ebc-495e-a4dc-6dee95742c78).

```{r worked-report, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_pain_report_example(report_example)
```

The accompanying [R code and software record](#sample-size-report-methods) reproduce the calculation: `r report_example$facts$analyzable` analyzable patients per group, followed by the 5% loss adjustment to `r report_example$facts$recruitment` recruits per group.

<details class="report-methods" id="sample-size-report-methods">
<summary>Calculation procedure and software record</summary>

The neuropathic pain calculation in the example report uses R `r report_example$r_version` and stats `r report_example$stats_version`. `stats::` identifies the package supplying `power.prop.test()`. Setting `strict = TRUE` includes rejection in either direction of the two-sided test. The [methods record](#tutorial-methods) explains the analysis and confidence interval used in the simulation app.

```{r report-command}
# Calculate patients per group for the specified event probabilities and power.
plan <- stats::power.prop.test(
  p1 = 0.60, p2 = 0.30, sig.level = 0.05, power = 0.90,
  alternative = "two.sided", strict = TRUE)
# $n extracts the calculated count; ceiling() rounds it upward to a whole patient.
analyzable_per_group <- ceiling(plan$n)
# Allow for 5% unavailable outcomes, rounding within each group.
recruit_per_group <- ceiling(analyzable_per_group / 0.95)
# c() collects the named results to display together.
c(unrounded_per_group = plan$n,
  analyzable_per_group = analyzable_per_group,
  analyzable_total = 2 * analyzable_per_group,
  recruit_per_group = recruit_per_group,
  recruit_total = 2 * recruit_per_group)
```

The [report activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/assumptions_report/?stage=calculation) includes the prepared calculation's software record when the neuropathic pain comparison is selected. An attached calculator result retains the inputs and software used for that result. The [reproducibility section](#reproducibility-record) explains the full record.

</details>


```{r consider-report-method, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_consider_check("consider-report-method")
```

Computational reproducibility means that another researcher can use the recorded inputs, procedure and software to obtain consistent results. Keeping the calculation, its evidence and dated decisions makes that check possible. Sharing suitable code and methods also supports scrutiny and reuse [@nas2019; @unesco2021].

## What belongs in the report? {#record-assumptions .core-heading}

Before completing the report, the method, inputs and result should be checked against an independent implementation or a documented benchmark. The section [Validating a sample size calculation](#validating-calculations) illustrates this check. Table \@ref(tab:planning-assumptions) is a checklist for Example 3.1 and the report activity. Each row connects one part of the report to the chapters that explain its decisions.

<span id="tab:report-annotations"></span>

::: {.planning-assumptions}

| Report part | What should be recorded and checked? |
|:--|:--|
| Question and design — [Chapter 1](#clinical-question) | PICO, eligibility and participant selection, treatment regimens and permitted additional care, primary outcome and assessment time. The allocation unit, ratio and dependence between observations should agree with the proposed analysis. |
| Assumptions and evidence — [Chapter 1](#clinical-question) and [Exploring power and uncertain assumptions](#curves) | The effect scale and direction, previous observations and their sources, clinical threshold and its justification, target difference, and both event percentages or the common SD. The evidence should be relevant to the patients, outcome and follow-up. Additional prompts cover uncertain inputs and plausible alternatives. |
| Calculation — [Chapter 2](#calculations) and [Methods and software to record](#reproducibility-record) | Planned test, sidedness and adjustments, Type I error probability, power at the specified difference, calculation procedure, software and versions. Unrounded and rounded analyzable counts should be given per group and in total. Estimation reports use a confidence level and precision target. Sources and reproducible commands should be retained. |
| Recruitment and conclusion — [Chapter 2](#calculations) | Expected unavailable outcomes and their justification, upward-rounded recruitment counts per group and in total, and how missing outcomes or treatment changes will be handled. Recruitment rates, time and resources should support feasibility. The intended conclusion should reflect the design and its statistical performance. |

Table: (\#tab:planning-assumptions) Checklist for the four parts of the sample size calculation report, with links to the relevant chapters and methods.

:::


```{r consider-report-evidence, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_consider_check("consider-report-evidence")
```

@wang2024bep illustrate how evidence supports numerical inputs, using local data for the control percentage and a systematic review for the target risk ratio. Your report should retain each source, its relevance and the plausible alternatives considered; [Chapter 5](#curves) develops that assessment.

Clear reporting also makes measurement choices open to scrutiny. In a review of 185 studies using the BREAST-Q Reconstruction Module, a patient-reported questionnaire for breast reconstruction, only 17 reported a sample-size calculation and 71 reported the primary outcome's assessment time; 36 had questionnaire-administration errors [@gallo2022]. These findings underline why your plan should specify how and when the outcome is measured alongside the calculation. Missing calculation details leave the sample-size justification unassessable. A review of 385 phase III oncology trials found that 41 (10.6%) cited previous clinical data to support the assumed hazard ratio. This concerns the evidence behind the numerical assumption, reinforcing the need to report both the calculation and the sources supporting its inputs [@noticewala2025effects].

<span id="report-statistical-criteria"></span>
<span id="report-calculation-method"></span>

The [optional mean-score report](#rehabilitation-report) gives the corresponding t-test example. [Estimation reporting](#estimation-report) uses a confidence level and precision target. Designs with several outcomes or interim decisions need the [additional design record](#complex-design-record).

<div class="chapter-recap">

### Take-home points {.unnumbered}

- The report should state what was calculated, why those inputs were chosen, and how the result can be reproduced.
- The sample size calculation report should explain the choice of assumptions and the consequence of a plausible alternative.
