# Sample size for estimation {#estimation-planning .advanced-heading}

::: {.learning-goals .advanced-outcomes}
After this chapter, you should be able to:

- Distinguish an estimate from the population quantity it describes.
- Explain confidence level, margin of error, interval width and the repeated-study meaning of a confidence interval.
- Justify the confidence level and precision target in relation to the study purpose.
- Plan a sample size for a desired precision and explain what its result means for patients or service planning.
- Write an estimation-based sample size calculation report with a justified precision target.
- Assess the precision available from an existing dataset or a pilot study.
:::

Suppose you are planning a neuropathy care service for adults with type 2 diabetes attending a diabetes clinic. How many of these patients have peripheral neuropathy? An estimate of that percentage would help the clinic anticipate its follow-up workload. Each sampled patient is assessed once, at enrollment.

A recent clinic study planned its neuropathy prevalence estimate using a 95% confidence level, an anticipated prevalence of 22%, and a five-percentage-point [margin of error](#margin-of-error) [@negussie2024]. The worked service plan below follows this approach using a planning assumption of 20%: about one patient in five. The aim is a 95% confidence interval roughly five percentage points either side of the estimate. Later sections consider a population mean, treatment differences, existing data and pilot retention.

## Estimates, confidence intervals and precision {#estimation-foundations .advanced-heading}

A sample estimate changes when different participants are sampled. A [confidence interval](#confidence-interval) uses the data and analysis assumptions to give a range describing uncertainty about the population quantity. A narrower interval indicates greater [precision](#precision) at the same confidence level.

Suppose a survey estimates neuropathy prevalence as 20%, with a symmetric 95% confidence interval from 15% to 25%. The margin of error is the distance from the estimate to either limit: 5 percentage points. The confidence interval is the whole range, 15% to 25%. Figure \@ref(fig:interval-margin) shows the two quantities side by side. The [full width](#full-width) is 25 minus 15, or 10 percentage points.

```{r interval-margin, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=3.7, fig.cap="The margin of error and confidence interval, using a survey estimate of 20% and a symmetric interval from 15% to 25%. The interval spans 10 percentage points; the margin of error is 5 percentage points on either side of the estimate.", fig.alt="Two panels share the same percentage scale. The left panel marks each five-percentage-point distance from the estimate of 20% to the limits as the margin of error. The right panel highlights the whole confidence interval from 15% to 25%."}
draw_interval_margin()
```

A 95% confidence level is a widely used convention. Its connection to the common 5% significance threshold follows from matching two-sided tests and confidence-interval procedures. Fisher helped popularize the 5% threshold in significance testing [@fisher1925methods]. The study purpose should determine the chosen confidence level [@nistconfidence].

The confidence level describes the statistical procedure used to calculate the interval from sample data. Imagine repeatedly sampling new patients from the same population and applying that procedure each time. If the procedure has 95% coverage under those assumptions, about 950 of 1,000 intervals would contain the population value. With more repetitions, the observed fraction tends toward the procedure's coverage probability. The population value stays fixed while the samples and their intervals change.

Each row in Figure \@ref(fig:twenty-prevalence-intervals) represents a separate simulated sample of 246 patients from the same clinic population, where 20% have neuropathy. Different samples include different patients, so the observed percentages vary. Each dot shows one sample's percentage; its horizontal line is a 95% confidence interval calculated from those patients to describe uncertainty about the population percentage.

The vertical line marks the known population value of 20%. In this illustrated batch, 19 green intervals contain it and one red interval misses it. The number containing it varies between batches. Over many such surveys, the fraction of intervals containing 20% would approach the coverage probability of this interval procedure. The clinic conducts one survey. Imagining many surveys explains what the confidence level describes.

```{r twenty-prevalence-intervals, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=6.4, fig.cap="Twenty simulated clinic samples of 246 adults, with population neuropathy prevalence fixed at 20%. Nineteen green intervals contain 20%; one red interval misses it. Circles and a cross distinguish the two outcomes as well as color. This batch illustrates the repeated-study meaning of 95% confidence.", fig.alt="Twenty horizontal confidence intervals around estimates from simulated clinic samples. A vertical line marks population neuropathy prevalence of 20%. Nineteen green intervals cross the line; one red interval, marked by a cross, lies entirely below it."}
draw_prevalence_coverage()
```

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-confidence-probability">
<summary>Common misconception: there is a 95% probability that prevalence lies between the observed limits of 15% and 25%</summary>

Those limits come from one survey. To understand 95% confidence, imagine 1,000 new surveys from the same population, each producing its own interval. A procedure with 95% coverage would include the population prevalence in about 950 of them. The fraction becomes more stable as more surveys are added. The particular interval from 15% to 25% either contains the population prevalence or misses it.

</details>

The clinic survey starts with a desired margin of error and confidence level, chosen for the service-planning decision. Higher confidence or a narrower target interval requires a larger sample under the same planning model. The next section turns that precision target into a total sample size.


```{r consider-margin, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_consider_check("consider-margin")
```

## Estimate one proportion: a prevalence survey {#prevalence .advanced-heading}

A prevalence survey estimates one population proportion at a defined time. Each participant contributes a binary outcome to one sample; you choose its size for a useful [margin of error](#margin-of-error).

Such estimates can inform service planning or recruitment and retention assumptions for a future trial. The planning question is how precisely the study should estimate the population percentage [@pourhoseingholi2013; @ying2025].

The clinic needs an estimate with a margin of error of five [percentage points](#percentage-points). Around an estimate of 20 patients per 100, this would give an interval extending approximately from 15 to 25 patients per 100. The service plan uses 95% confidence. Here, $n$ is the total number of independently sampled patients from the clinic register.

For an anticipated population proportion $p_0$, the normal approximation gives:

\begin{equation}
n\approx\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}^{2}p_0(1-p_0)}{d^2}.
(\#eq:single-proportion)
\end{equation}

Here $p_0$ is the anticipated population proportion and $d$ is the desired margin of error, both entered as decimals. At 95% confidence, the standard-normal cutoff is approximately $z_{1-\alpha/2}=1.96$. Substituting 20% prevalence and a margin of 5 percentage points into Equation \@ref(eq:single-proportion) gives:

\begin{equation}
n\approx\frac{1.96^2\times0.20\times(1-0.20)}{0.05^2}
=\frac{3.8416\times0.20\times0.80}{0.0025}
=245.86.
(\#eq:prevalence-worked)
\end{equation}

Rounding upward gives 246 completed assessments. The clinic would select patients from its register and aim to obtain this many completed neuropathy assessments. The planned precision would help estimate follow-up workload to within about five affected patients per 100 clinic patients.

The same clinic can compare confidence levels while keeping the five-percentage-point margin fixed:

```{r confidence-level-counts, echo=FALSE}
levels <- c(.90, .95, .99)
# qnorm() supplies the normal cutoff for each confidence level.
assessments <- ceiling(qnorm((1 + levels) / 2)^2 * .20 * .80 / .05^2)
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Confidence level` = percent(levels),
  `Completed assessments` = assessments, check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Completed neuropathy assessments required at different confidence levels, assuming 20% prevalence and a five-percentage-point margin of error. Counts use the normal approximation.")
```

Higher confidence requires more assessments to preserve the same margin. With a fixed sample, higher confidence produces a wider interval. Greater precision can be obtained through more observations or a more efficient design. More reliable coverage can require a better interval method, as the [Wilson interval illustration](#wilson-interval) shows. The confidence level and useful margin should be chosen together before examining the results [@nistconfidence]. For another clinic, the anticipated prevalence and margin needed for service planning should be reconsidered.

If there is no useful prior estimate, 50% ($p_0=0.50$) gives the largest value of $p_0(1-p_0)$ and an approximate requirement of 385.

```{r single-proportion-precision}
# Plan for a full width of 10 percentage points at 95% confidence.
prevalence_known <- proportion_precision_plan(p = .20,
  full_width = .10, confidence = .95)
# unknown_p = TRUE uses 50%, the conservative value for this approximation.
prevalence_unknown <- proportion_precision_plan(p = .20,
  full_width = .10, confidence = .95, unknown_p = TRUE)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Scenario = c("Prior estimate 20%", "Unknown: use 50% for planning"),
  `Assumed population percentage` = percent(c(prevalence_known$planning_p,
    prevalence_unknown$planning_p)),
  `Completed observations` = c(prevalence_known$n, prevalence_unknown$n),
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Approximate prevalence sample sizes for a 95% interval with a 5-percentage-point margin of error.")
```

The conservative 50% choice concerns absolute precision for one proportion under this approximation. For a rare outcome, an absolute margin of five percentage points might be unhelpfully wide; event counts and the chosen interval method also matter.

Reducing the margin of error from 5 to 2.5 percentage points requires about four times as many completed assessments under this formula. The app below applies these choices to the neuropathy survey and shows an interval from a simulated sample. The [methods table](#tutorial-methods) identifies its planning formula and analysis interval.

```{r prevalence-app-preview, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_app_preview("prevalence", "Compare sample sizes and confidence interval widths for one population percentage.")
```

The survey's anticipated prevalence, confidence level, margin of error and required participant count can now be brought together in a sample size calculation report.

## Reporting an estimation-based sample size {#estimation-report .advanced-heading}

An estimation plan identifies the population quantity, outcome and assessment time, confidence level, desired full interval width, anticipated percentages or SD, interval method, software and participant counts. Its justification explains why the chosen width would be useful. For existing data, it describes the available count and anticipated precision. The [report activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/assumptions_report/?stage=calculation) displays these fields when an estimation goal is selected; [Chapter 3](#reporting) explains the common report structure.

The report below follows the study-size and statistical-method reporting items in STROBE and the precision-based approach in the published neuropathy study [@strobe2007; @negussie2024].

The normal approximation gives an initial sample size from the anticipated percentage and desired margin. The completed survey will use a [Wilson score interval](#wilson-interval), which stays within 0% and 100% and allows different margins on either side of the estimate. It is based on a [score test](#score-test). The glossary illustration compares Wilson and normal intervals using the same patient counts [@brown2001interval]. The report records the planning method and analysis interval separately.

<div class="annotated-report" id="estimation-report-example" role="group" aria-labelledby="estimation-report-caption">

<p class="caption" id="estimation-report-caption">Example 4.1. Sample size calculation report for the neuropathy prevalence survey.</p>

<p class="report-part">Question and design</p>

<span class="report-mark">Research question and population:</span> What percentage of adults with type 2 diabetes attending the clinic have peripheral neuropathy? <span class="report-mark">Outcome and sampling:</span> Peripheral neuropathy will be assessed once per patient at enrollment using the same diagnostic criteria. A simple random sample will be drawn from the clinic register, with one observation per patient.

<p class="report-part">Assumptions and evidence</p>

<span class="report-mark">Anticipated prevalence:</span> The calculation uses 20%, approximately one patient in five, informed by the clinic study motivating this service plan [@negussie2024]. <span class="report-mark">Precision target:</span> A 95% confidence interval with a margin of error of five percentage points is intended to support workload planning to within approximately five affected patients per 100 clinic patients. Its full width is ten percentage points. <span class="report-mark">Sensitivity analysis:</span> An anticipated prevalence of 25% would require 289 completed assessments under the same normal approximation. The selected prevalence and its relevance to the clinic population will be reviewed before recruitment.

<p class="report-part">Calculation</p>

<span class="report-mark">Planning procedure and software:</span> The single-proportion normal approximation uses $n=z_{0.975}^2p(1-p)/d^2$, with $p=0.20$ and $d=0.05$, implemented in R `r getRversion()` with `stats::qnorm(0.975)`. <span class="report-mark">Required sample:</span> The unrounded result is 245.85336, rounded upward to 246 completed assessments in total. <span class="report-mark">Planned analysis:</span> The observed percentage will be reported with a two-sided 95% Wilson score interval without continuity correction. The planning formula, inputs and software record are retained with the report.

<p class="report-part">Recruitment and conclusion</p>

<span class="report-mark">Nonresponse:</span> Allowing for five nonparticipants per 100 invited patients gives $\lceil246/0.95\rceil=259$ eligible patients to approach. <span class="report-mark">Feasibility:</span> The clinic register and appointment schedule will be checked for this number of eligible patients. <span class="report-mark">Intended use:</span> The prevalence estimate and its interval will inform the number of patients likely to need neuropathy care in a comparable clinic population.

</div>

To interpret a result for workload planning, an estimated prevalence of 20% would correspond to about 200 affected patients in a comparable clinic population of 1,000. An interval from 15% to 25% would correspond to approximately 150–250 affected patients.

The following draft concerns a different service question: the percentage of clinic patients needing an interpreter. Apply the same reporting principles to its new assumptions and counts. Select the highlighted passages to inspect the calculation and reporting problems.

```{r estimation-report-error, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_error_activity("estimation_report")
```

## Estimating a population mean {#plan-for-precision .advanced-heading}

The same precision-based approach can be used for a population mean, with the SD describing variability between patients.

A rehabilitation study aims to estimate the mean improvement in one patient population. You should specify how narrow the confidence interval needs to be to support a useful interpretation. Here, a 95% confidence interval with an anticipated full width of 4 score units is the precision target [@wang2020; @lakens2022].

For an initial normal approximation, the margin of error $d$ is $z_{1-\alpha/2}\sigma/\sqrt{n}$, so:

\begin{equation}
n\approx\left(\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}\sigma}{d}\right)^2.
(\#eq:single-mean-precision)
\end{equation}

With SD $\sigma=5$ and a margin of 2 score units (full width 4), substituting into Equation \@ref(eq:single-mean-precision) gives:

\begin{equation}
n\approx\left(\frac{1.96\times5}{2}\right)^2=24.01
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n=25.
(\#eq:single-mean-worked)
\end{equation}

The researchers would initially plan for 25 completed assessments. The app refines this calculation for a t interval, allowing for estimation of the SD from the sample. Its expected-width criterion requires 26 completed assessments, as explained below.

With an assumed SD of 5 units, [Activity: Estimate a population mean with a precision target](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/book/estimation-planning.html#activity-mean_precision) finds the smallest total sample meeting this target. The calculation uses the confidence level, SD and desired width. The population mean used in simulation is 3 units, which supplies a known value for checking the intervals.

```{r precision-plan}
# Define one population and the desired precision for its mean.
# The mean of 3 supplies a known value for checking interval coverage.
precision_spec <- single_population_spec(outcome = "means", mean = 3,
  sd = 5, confidence = .95, width = 4, B = 5000, seed = 20260922)
# Find the smallest total sample meeting the expected interval-width target.
precision_n <- single_population_n(precision_spec)
c(analyzable_total = precision_n,
  anticipated_full_width = single_population_width(precision_spec, precision_n))
# Repeated samples produce different estimates and interval widths.
precision_batch <- single_population_simulate(precision_spec, precision_n, many = TRUE)
```

```{r precision-plan-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable participants (total)`=precision_n, `Anticipated full interval width`=round(single_population_width(precision_spec, precision_n),2),check.names=FALSE), caption="Total sample required to estimate one population mean with a 95% confidence interval of anticipated full width at most 4 score units, assuming SD 5.")
```

The calculation requires `r precision_n` completed observations in total. A full width of four score units corresponds to roughly two units on either side of the estimated mean. For normal data, this calculation uses the expected full width of a t interval. The normal approximation supplies an initial explanation of the relationship between SD, precision and sample size. Realized widths vary with the sample SD. The simulation shows how often intervals contain the known population mean and how often their width meets the chosen target [@sandoval2025].

<details class="advanced-explanation" id="mean-width-calculation">
<summary>How the app calculates expected interval width</summary>

A sample of $n$ observations gives the interval $\bar x\pm t_{0.975,n-1}s/\sqrt n$, with full width $2t_{0.975,n-1}s/\sqrt n$. The sample SD $s$ changes between samples. Under normal sampling, its expectation is $\sigma c_4(n-1)$, where $c_4(\nu)=\sqrt{2/\nu}\,\Gamma((\nu+1)/2)/\Gamma(\nu/2)$, $\nu$ (nu) denotes degrees of freedom and $\Gamma$ (capital gamma) is the gamma function. The app finds the smallest integer $n$ for which $2t_{0.975,n-1}\sigma c_4(n-1)/\sqrt n$ is at most 4. Its result concerns the expected width across samples. The [methods table](#tutorial-methods) records this criterion alongside the other calculations.

</details>

```{r precision-app-preview, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_app_preview("mean_precision", "Explore sample size for a chosen confidence interval width.")
```


```{r consider-interval-width, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_consider_check("consider-interval-width")
```



## Clinical interpretation of a confidence interval {#interpret-a-confidence-interval-clinically .advanced-heading}

To interpret one trial, you can compare its confidence interval with both zero and the 20-percentage-point clinical threshold introduced for the neuropathic pain trial. Zero represents no population difference; the clinical threshold represents the between-group benefit judged worthwhile in this example.

The neuropathic pain trial illustrates a further use of estimation: interpreting a between-group difference after a trial planned for power. The following three intervals show how the conclusion depends on the values compatible with the data.

```{r clinical-intervals, echo=FALSE}
clinical_intervals <- data.frame(
  lower_pp = c(2, -8, 22),
  upper_pp = c(28, 32, 42),
  interpretation = c(
    "The interval excludes zero and includes benefits below and above the 20 point threshold.",
    "Some harm, no difference, small benefits and clinically important benefits remain compatible with the data.",
    "All values in the interval exceed 20 percentage points under the analysis assumptions."),
  plot_label = c("Benefit; clinical\nimportance uncertain",
    "Inconclusive\ncomparison", "Benefit above\nclinical threshold"))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `Interval for the difference in relief` = paste(clinical_intervals$lower_pp,
    "to", clinical_intervals$upper_pp, "percentage points"),
  `Clinical conclusion` = c("Benefit with uncertain clinical importance", "Inconclusive comparison", "Benefit above the clinical threshold"),
  Explanation = clinical_intervals$interpretation,
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Hypothetical 95% intervals for novel minus standard treatment, compared with zero and a 20-percentage-point clinical threshold.")
```

Figure \@ref(fig:clinical-interval-plot) places the intervals in Table \@ref(tab:clinical-intervals) on the same scale. Positive differences favor the novel treatment. You can see whether each interval crosses zero, crosses the clinical threshold, or lies entirely below it.

```{r clinical-interval-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.6, fig.cap="Three hypothetical 95% confidence intervals on a common scale. The solid vertical line marks no between-group difference; the dashed line marks the 20-percentage-point clinical threshold. Each horizontal bar spans the stated interval limits.", fig.alt="Three horizontal confidence intervals for novel minus standard treatment. The interval from 2 to 28 percentage points excludes zero but crosses the clinical threshold of 20. The interval from minus 8 to 32 crosses both zero and 20. The interval from 22 to 42 lies entirely above 20."}
par(mar = c(5, 9.1, 4.3, 1), las = 1, bg = "white",
  fg = "#26343d", col.axis = "#26343d", col.lab = "#26343d")
plot(NA, xlim = c(-12, 48), ylim = c(.55, 3.55),
  xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i", axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
interval_rows <- 3:1
abline(h = interval_rows, col = "#e5e9ec", lwd = 1)
abline(v = 0, col = "#4b5560", lwd = 1.5)
abline(v = 20, col = "#72428b", lwd = 1.8, lty = 2)
axis(1, at = seq(-10, 40, 10), cex.axis = .95)
mtext("Difference in pain-relief percentages", side = 1, line = 2.4)
mtext("Novel minus standard treatment (percentage points)", side = 1,
  line = 3.6, cex = .85)
text(c(0, 20), 3.67, c("No difference\n0", "Clinical threshold\n20"),
  adj = c(.5, 0), cex = .85, xpd = NA)
text(-14, interval_rows, clinical_intervals$plot_label,
  adj = 1, cex = .9, xpd = NA)
segments(clinical_intervals$lower_pp, interval_rows,
  clinical_intervals$upper_pp, interval_rows,
  col = "#17658a", lwd = 3, lend = "butt")
for (limits in list(clinical_intervals$lower_pp, clinical_intervals$upper_pp)) {
  segments(limits, interval_rows - .09, limits, interval_rows + .09,
    col = "#17658a", lwd = 2)
  text(limits, interval_rows + .19, labels = limits, cex = .85)
}
```

For a $100(1-\alpha)$% confidence interval and its corresponding two sided test, excluding zero indicates statistical significance at level $\alpha$. Thus 90% confidence corresponds to 10% significance, 95% to 5%, and 99% to 1%. This correspondence requires the interval to be constructed from that test. Chapter 6 explains why [different test and interval procedures](#activity-3-generate-analyze-repeat-summarize) can disagree. Clinical interpretation also depends on whether the interval lies below, crosses, or lies entirely above the clinical threshold.

The confidence intervals in Figure \@ref(fig:clinical-interval-plot) concern the population difference between treatment groups. See [Between-group differences and individual benefit](#between-group-differences) for the implications for individual patients.

Clinical interpretation also considers harms, burden, and the credibility of the study [@sandoval2025].

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-power-precision">
<summary>Common misconception: 90% power means the trial will show whether the pain relief is large enough to matter</summary>

The neuropathic pain trial is planned to detect a difference if the true benefit is 30 additional patients with relief per 100 treated. Suppose its observed interval instead runs from 2 to 28 additional patients per 100, as in Figure \@ref(fig:clinical-interval-plot). That result supports a treatment difference, while leaving uncertainty about whether it exceeds the clinical threshold of 20 per 100. Planning for power and planning for a narrow interval answer different questions.

</details>

## Reuse an existing dataset for a different question {#dataset-reuse .advanced-heading}

An existing dataset provides a fixed resource for a new question in a student project, clinical service evaluation or research study. Suppose a completed neuropathic pain trial included 200 patients and also recorded sleep difficulty before treatment. Your new question is: what percentage of these trial participants reported sleep difficulty at baseline? This differs from the trial's original question about treatment effectiveness.

Baseline sleep information is available for 180 participants; 72 reported difficulty. The observed percentage is 72/180 = 40%. With the sample already fixed, the planning task is to assess the precision the available data can provide.

```{r reused-dataset}
# Estimate a percentage and interval from 72 events among 180 observations.
sleep_result <- single_proportion_interval(events = 72, n = 180,
  confidence = .95)
sleep_result
```

```{r reused-dataset-summary, echo=FALSE}
sleep_limits <- wilson_interval(.40, 180)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Measure = c("Patients in the dataset", "With baseline sleep information",
    "Reporting sleep difficulty", "Observed percentage", "95% Wilson confidence interval"),
  Result = c("200", "180", "72", "40.0%",
    paste(percent(sleep_limits[1, 1]), "to", percent(sleep_limits[1, 2])))),
  caption = "A new descriptive question answered using an existing neuropathic pain trial dataset.")
```

The estimate corresponds to 40 patients reporting sleep difficulty per 100, with an interval from about `r round(100*sleep_limits[1, 1])` to `r round(100*sleep_limits[1, 2])` per 100 under the model. This supports a broad description; a decision needing a margin of two patients per 100 would require greater precision. Possible differences between the 20 patients with missing information and those who answered require separate assessment. The trial's eligibility criteria also restrict whom these results describe: its participants may not represent all patients with neuropathic pain. Random allocation supports the original treatment comparison.

Before analyzing the reused data, you should check that the required variables and time points are available, reuse is permitted, and the analysis fits the new objective. Your report should state the precision needed for the decision and identify analyses developed after inspecting the data as exploratory [@lakens2022; @consortee2025].



```{r consider-reuse-precision, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_consider_check("consider-reuse-precision")
```



## Planning a pilot or feasibility study {#pilot-feasibility .advanced-heading}

So far, feasibility has meant whether you can carry out an informative main study. A preliminary pilot or feasibility study has its own research objectives: investigating whether recruitment, retention, delivery, or other procedures will work. Its sample size should support those decisions.

Suppose a team wants to test a new rehabilitation pathway and needs evidence about recruitment and follow-up. It can recruit 40 patients over three months to investigate these procedures.

Here the sample size should support decisions about recruitment, retention and delivery. Before starting, specify [progression criteria](#progression-criteria): conditions used to decide whether to proceed, modify the procedures or stop. These might concern recruitment per month, retention at the required visit and whether the intervention can be delivered as intended [@eldridge2016]. The section [Choosing plausible assumptions in Chapter 5](#st01-expectations) explains how pilot findings and other evidence inform planning for the main trial [@albers2018].

For the pilot, your plan should connect the available resources with the precision needed for these feasibility decisions. The [single-proportion example](#prevalence) explains the corresponding interval-width calculation. Here the hypothetical cap is 40 participants, and expected completion of follow-up is 80%. With 32 of 40 completing follow-up, the observed retention and its interval are shown below.

```{r pilot-retention}
# Estimate retention and its interval from 32 completions among 40 participants.
pilot_retention <- single_proportion_interval(events = 32, n = 40,
  confidence = .95)
pilot_retention
```

```{r pilot-retention-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Completed follow-up`="32/40 (80%)", `95% Wilson confidence interval`=paste(percent(pilot_retention$lower), "to", percent(pilot_retention$upper)), check.names=FALSE), caption="Retention and its uncertainty in a 40-participant feasibility study.")
```

The observed 80% retention still has a wide interval. You can compare it with a prospectively agreed progression criterion and consider reasons for missing outcomes. A point estimate of 80% alone cannot establish that the main trial will retain at least 80%.

Your pilot size should reflect the decision it must support. Ying and colleagues distinguish estimating feasibility with useful precision, assessing progression criteria, detecting practical problems and informing variability for the main trial [@ying2025]. You should specify each outcome's denominator: retention concerns participants enrolled, while a recruitment percentage may concern eligible people approached.

The app below starts with 40 participants and an 80% retention probability. Comparing samples of 40 and 100 shows how more observations affect the uncertainty in the retention estimate. Both retained and non-retained participants contribute when their status is known.

```{r pilot-app-preview, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_app_preview("pilot_feasibility", "Explore the information a pilot with a fixed number of participants can provide.")
```


```{r consider-pilot-progression, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_consider_check("consider-pilot-progression")
```



For another objective, suppose a practical problem independently affects 10% of participants. The probability of observing at least one problem in $n$ participants is $1-(1-0.10)^n$; 29 give at least a 95% probability. Much rarer problems require larger samples for reliable detection. A problem can remain undetected in a small pilot [@ying2025]. Different pilot objectives can therefore imply different numbers.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-pilot-goal">
<summary>Common misconception: every pilot study must be sized to detect a treatment effect with high power</summary>

A pilot may primarily investigate recruitment, retention or whether procedures are workable. The sample size should support the feasibility questions and provide useful precision for the intended decisions. Planning the definitive trial should combine the pilot findings with relevant external evidence [@albers2018].

</details>

Before writing the protocol, you should check relevant guidance and the current funder's requirements. For examples, [NIHR HTA guidance on feasibility and pilot studies](https://njl-admin.nihr.ac.uk/document/download/2023130) distinguishes feasibility questions from definitive efficacy questions; this is an archived guidance example. The [CONSORT extension for randomized pilot and feasibility trials](https://www.bmj.com/content/355/bmj.i5239) asks for a rationale for pilot numbers and criteria for progression [@nihrfeasibility; @eldridge2016]. Reporting guidance helps you document the design. The sample size method should match the study question and planned analysis.

<div class="chapter-recap">

### Take-home points {.unnumbered}

- An estimate describes a population quantity using sample data; its confidence interval expresses uncertainty.
- A precision target specifies confidence level and interval width. Higher confidence requires more observations to keep the same margin of error.
- Estimation can concern a single population or a between-group difference.
- The justification should explain why the interval width supports the intended decision.

</div>

## Check your understanding {#check-estimation .unnumbered}

```{r quiz-estimation, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_chapter_quiz("estimation-planning")
```

# Exploring power and uncertain assumptions {#curves .advanced-heading}

::: {.learning-goals .advanced-outcomes}
After this chapter, you should be able to:

- Read power at a selected sample size and the sample required for a selected power target from the same curves.
- Justify plausible assumptions using relevant evidence and its uncertainty.
- Compare fixed-assumption power, assurance and a Bayesian success criterion using the neuropathic pain example.
- Assess how event probabilities, outcome variability and available sample size affect power.
- Evaluate feasible design changes when the available sample provides insufficient power.

:::

The [neuropathic pain calculation in Chapter 2](#two-proportions) planned for 60% relief with the novel treatment and 30% with standard treatment, a target difference of 30 percentage points. Here, you will examine how power changes if the true difference is smaller or recruitment limits the available sample. Suppose the neuropathic pain trial can provide 100 analyzable patients per group. The question is what that sample could detect, and which assumptions most affect the answer. Start by reading power at a fixed patient count. Then examine the evidence for the assumptions, vary uncertain inputs and consider what to do if the sample is insufficient. The expandable explanation of hypothesis tests supplies additional detail when needed.

## Reading power curves {#activity-2-can-the-feasible-study-answer-the-question .advanced-heading}

Table \@ref(tab:cap-table) gives three concrete planning scenarios. Figure \@ref(fig:power-curves) then shows how their power changes across sample sizes. Standard-treatment relief stays at 30%; novel-treatment relief is 45%, 50% or 60%, giving differences of 15, 20 or 30 percentage points. Each curve describes repeated trials under one set of population assumptions [@superpowerbook2022].

The vertical line marks the available 100 analyzable patients per group. The horizontal line marks 90% target power. Recruitment should allow for expected losses separately, using the [recruitment calculation](#account-for-expected-losses).

```{r curve-settings}
# Specify the population assumptions and the available analysis count.
analyzable_cap <- 100
curve_spec <- study_spec(outcome = "proportions", n = analyzable_cap,
  p_control = .30, p_treatment = .60, threshold = .20,
  width_target = .20)
# Compare three true between-group differences, expressed as probabilities.
effect_sizes <- c(.15, .20, .30)
target_power <- .90
```

```{r cap-table, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cap_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(effect_sizes, function(effect) {
  x <- curve_spec; x$p_treatment <- x$p_control + effect
  data.frame(difference = 100 * effect,
    power = percent(spec_power(x, analyzable_cap)),
    required = plan_n(x, target_power = target_power))
}))
cap_labels <- if (knitr::is_html_output()) {
  c("&#9679; Power with 100 per group", "&#9675; Patients per group for 90% power")
} else {
  c("$\\bullet$ Power with 100 per group", "$\\circ$ Patients per group for 90% power")
}
knitr::kable(cap_results, escape = FALSE,
  format = if (knitr::is_html_output()) "html" else "latex",
  col.names = c("True difference (percentage points)", cap_labels),
  caption = "Power with 100 analyzable patients per group and sample size required for 90% power.")
```

```{r power-curves, fig.width=8, fig.height=5.8, fig.cap="Power for true treatment differences of 15, 20 and 30 percentage points, with standard-treatment relief of 30% and two-sided Type I error probability of 5%. Reference lines mark 90% target power and 100 analyzable patients per group.", fig.alt="Power rises with patients per group. At the vertical line of 100, power is about 59%, 83% and 99% for the three differences. The curves reach the horizontal 90% target at 217, 124 and 56 patients per group, respectively."}
# Include all three crossings of the power target in the horizontal range.
curve_table <- power_curve_data(curve_spec, effect_sizes, seq(5, 250, 1))
plot_power_curves(curve_table, target_power, analyzable_cap)
```

<span id="hold-sample-size-fixed-and-vary-the-effect"></span>
<span id="fig:effect-curve"></span>


In Table \@ref(tab:cap-table) and Figure \@ref(fig:power-curves), filled circles identify power at the vertical line of 100 patients per group. Open circles identify the patient counts where each curve reaches the horizontal line of 90% power. For the 20 point difference, the filled circle gives about 83% power at 100 patients per group. The open circle gives 124 patients per group for 90% power. Smaller differences are harder to distinguish from sampling variation. Increasing the sample reduces that variation, helping the test detect a smaller difference. [Chapter 2](#how-error-rates-and-power-affect-sample-size) explains this relationship.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-detection-boundary">
<summary>Common misconception: a trial planned for a 30-point benefit cannot detect a 20-point benefit</summary>

A 20-point benefit can produce a statistically significant result. With 100 patients per group in Figure \@ref(fig:power-curves), power is about 99% at a true 30-point benefit, 83% at 20 points and 59% at 15 points. The target difference identifies where power was evaluated when choosing the sample size.

</details>

The [Sample size reasoning lab](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/book/curves.html#activity-pain_curves) starts with 100 analyzable patients per group. Clicking its graph can select an available sample or a target power. The reference lines, marked crossings and table update together. The input fields provide the same choices with a keyboard. The axes stay fixed during comparisons, with an option to show crossings outside the current range.

```{r power-app-preview, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_app_preview("pain_curves", "Compare power for plausible treatment differences with 100 analyzable patients per group.")
```


```{r consider-power-curve, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_consider_check("consider-power-curve")
```



<span id="model-answer-curve-assumptions"></span>
<span id="model-answer-curves-justify"></span>

<details class="advanced-explanation" id="testing-mechanics">
<summary>How hypothesis tests produce power</summary>

The following examples connect an individual test result to the repeated-study probabilities represented by power curves.

### Does the pilot already answer the clinical question? {#critical-observed-difference .advanced-heading}

For this two-sided comparison, the p-value answers: if the treatments truly had equal population relief probabilities, how likely would the chosen test be to produce a result at least as far from equality as the one observed, in either direction? This calculation also assumes that the statistical model is appropriate. A small p-value provides evidence against equal population relief probabilities under the statistical model.

The pilot's observed 40-percentage-point difference exceeds the 20-percentage-point [clinical threshold](#clinical-threshold). But the estimate is uncertain. Using a two-sided comparison of proportions gives a p-value of approximately 0.074. With a Type I error probability of 5%, this does not provide sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis using the chosen test.

What would happen with one more response? If relief with standard treatment remained at 3 of 10 patients, while relief with novel treatment increased from 7 to 8 of 10, the observed difference would increase from 40 to 50 percentage points:

```{r pain-critical-p-values, warning=FALSE}
# Compare the pilot result with one additional treatment response
pain_p_value <- function(novel, standard, n) {
  # x gives relief counts; n gives group sizes. correct = FALSE omits continuity correction.
  prop.test(
    x = c(novel, standard),
    n = c(n, n),
    alternative = "two.sided",
    correct = FALSE
  )$p.value
}

# Compare the two observed results; round p-values to three decimal places.
round(c(
  "7 versus 3" = pain_p_value(7, 3, 10),
  "8 versus 3" = pain_p_value(8, 3, 10)
), 3)
```

```{r pain-critical-p-values-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Novel treatment` = c("7/10 (70%)", "8/10 (80%)"), `Standard treatment` = "3/10 (30%)", `Observed difference` = c("40 percentage points", "50 percentage points"), `p-value` = formatC(c(pain_p_value(7,3,10), pain_p_value(8,3,10)), format="f", digits=3), check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Pilot comparisons with seven or eight responses to the novel treatment.")
```

With 8 rather than 7 patients reporting relief, the result becomes statistically significant. For this particular comparison, the smallest observed difference giving $p<0.05$ is therefore $0.8-0.3=0.5$, or 50 [percentage points](#percentage-points).

Notice that the [clinical threshold](#clinical-threshold) remains 20 percentage points. What patients would consider a worthwhile improvement does not change because your pilot happens to contain only 10 patients per group.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-significance">
<summary>Common misconception: a statistically significant benefit must be large enough to matter to patients</summary>

An interval of 2 to 28 additional patients with relief per 100 treated excludes no benefit. It also includes benefits below the 20-per-100 clinical threshold. Statistical significance alone leaves that clinical judgment unresolved. The section [Clinical interpretation of a confidence interval](#interpret-a-confidence-interval-clinically) compares these values visually.

</details>

*The pilot p-value calculation in [Does the pilot already answer the clinical question?](#critical-observed-difference) uses an approximate test without [continuity correction](#continuity-correction), matching the [Sample size reasoning lab](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/book/clinical-question.html#activity-pain_one_many). With such small groups, an exact test may give a different result.*

#### What happens if you recruit more patients? {.advanced-heading}

You can repeat the pilot comparison of pain relief percentages for larger studies. At each sample size, the observed percentage reporting relief with standard treatment stays at 30%. The calculation identifies the smallest number reporting relief with the novel treatment that gives $p<0.05$.

```{r pain-critical-effect, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.height=5.8, fig.cap="Smallest observed improvement giving p < 0.05 at each sample size, conditional on an observed control response of 30%. The two-sided score test uses no continuity correction. Points represent attainable patient counts; connecting lines guide the eye. The hypothetical clinical threshold is 20 percentage points. Counts are analyzable patients before adjustment for dropout.", fig.alt="The smallest observed difference giving statistical significance falls from 50 percentage points at 10 patients per group to 14 at 100 per group. A horizontal line marks the clinical threshold of 20 percentage points. The pilot difference of 40 points at 10 patients per group lies below the significance threshold."}
pain_n <- seq(10, 100, by = 10)
pain_critical <- vapply(pain_n, function(n) {
  control <- as.integer(round(0.30 * n))
  treatment <- seq.int(control + 1L, n)
  p <- vapply(treatment, function(x) pain_p_value(x, control, n), numeric(1))
  min((treatment[p < 0.05] - control) / n)
}, numeric(1))

local({
  old_par <- par(mar = c(5, 5, 2, 1), las = 1)
  on.exit(par(old_par))
  plot(pain_n, 100 * pain_critical, type = "b", pch = 16, lwd = 2,
       col = "#17658A", ylim = c(0, 66), xaxt = "n",
       xlab = "Analyzable patients per group (equal allocation)",
       ylab = "Observed difference in pain relief (percentage points)")
  axis(1, at = pain_n)
  abline(h = 20, col = "#A5500C", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
  points(10, 40, pch = 1, cex = 1.5, lwd = 2, col = "#303A43")
  legend("topright",
         c("Smallest observed difference with p < 0.05",
           "Clinical threshold: 20 percentage points",
           "Pilot: 7/10 versus 3/10"),
         col = c("#17658A", "#A5500C", "#303A43"),
         lty = c(1, 2, NA), pch = c(16, NA, 1),
         lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
})
```

With 20 patients per group, an observed difference of 35 percentage points is sufficient for statistical significance under these conditions. With 50 patients per group, the corresponding difference is 20 percentage points. As the sample size increases, smaller observed differences can therefore become statistically significant.

Figure \@ref(fig:pain-critical-effect) shows how the observed significance boundary changes. The dashed line shows the clinically meaningful difference chosen for this example. With a larger sample, a result can be statistically significant even when the observed difference is smaller than this clinical threshold. You therefore need to consider the size of the difference and its confidence interval when interpreting the result.

#### How does this relate to power? {.advanced-heading}

The significance boundary concerns an observed result. [Power](#statistical-power) concerns the performance of the planned study: *If the true treatment difference is 30 percentage points, how likely is your study to produce a statistically significant result?*

Different samples will give different observed differences, even when the true treatment effect remains the same. Some will be larger and others smaller. A power calculation takes this variation into account. The [simulation activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/book/clinical-question.html#activity-pain_one_many) estimates this probability by counting how many of thousands of trials detect a difference.

The observed significance boundary and the true difference used to evaluate power answer different questions [@lakens2022; @superpowerbook2022]. The [clinical interpretation of the interval](#interpret-a-confidence-interval-clinically) considers whether benefits below the clinical threshold remain compatible with the data.

### Type I and Type II error probabilities as areas {#alpha-beta .advanced-heading}

This separate example uses one group to make the error probabilities easier to draw. Imagine repeatedly sampling 25 patients and calculating their mean systolic blood pressure. Imagine collecting thousands of such samples and plotting one mean from each. The curves describe the distribution approached as more sample means are added. One curve assumes a population mean of 120 mmHg; the other assumes 125 mmHg. These are sampling distributions of the mean.

[Standard deviation](#standard-deviation){.no-glossary-tooltip} (SD) describes how much individual patients differ. [Standard error](#standard-error){.no-glossary-tooltip} (SE) describes how much an estimated mean would vary if you repeated the study with new patients. The individual blood pressures vary within each sample, while the mean varies between samples. If individual blood pressures have a known SD of 15 mmHg, the mean from 25 independent patients has an SE of $15/\sqrt{25}=3$ mmHg. With 100 patients, the SE falls to 1.5 mmHg. Increasing the sample size reduces the standard error of the mean while the population SD remains fixed.

For this illustration, the null hypothesis specifies a mean of 120 mmHg. A one-sided test looks for an increase, rejecting the null when the sample mean exceeds a cutoff called the critical value. The [two-arm treatment-comparison activities](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/book/clinical-question.html#activity-pain_one_many) use [two-sided tests](#two-sided-test).

Under the 120 mmHg curve, the area above the cutoff is the probability of a false positive: the [Type I error probability](#alpha). Under the 125 mmHg curve, the area below the cutoff is the probability of a false negative: the [Type II error probability](#beta). The area under the alternative curve above the cutoff is the true-positive probability, or power. Figure \@ref(fig:sampling-distribution-figure) separates the two assumed populations so that each shaded area has an unambiguous interpretation.

```{r alpha-beta-areas}
# Population means under the null and the specified alternative.
mu0 <- 120
mu1 <- 125
sigma <- 15
n <- 25
alpha <- .05
# sqrt(n) is the square root of n; the mean varies less as n increases.
standard_error <- sigma / sqrt(n)
# For this one-sided example, qnorm() gives the rejection cutoff.
critical <- mu0 + qnorm(1 - alpha) * standard_error
# pnorm() gives the probability below that cutoff under the alternative.
# This is the Type II error probability; its complement is power.
beta <- pnorm(critical, mean = mu1, sd = standard_error)
c(standard_error = standard_error, critical = critical,
  beta = beta, power = 1 - beta)
```

```{r alpha-beta-areas-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Measure=c("Standard error", "Critical mean", "Type I error probability", "Type II error probability", "Power"), Result=c(paste(standard_error,"mmHg"), paste(round(critical,1),"mmHg"), percent(alpha), percent(beta), percent(1-beta))),
  caption = "Error probabilities and power for the specified sampling distributions.")
```

```{r sampling-distribution-figure, echo=FALSE, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Sampling distributions of the mean with 25 independent observations and known SD 15 mmHg. In the upper panel, the shaded rejection area is Type I error probability. In the lower panel, the shaded non-rejection area is Type II error probability and the shaded rejection area is power.", fig.alt="The upper null curve is centered at 120 and the lower alternative curve at 125 mmHg. Both have standard error 3. The critical mean is about 124.9; Type I error probability is 5 percent and Type II error probability about 49 percent."}
sampling_example <- normal_sampling_operating_characteristics(
  mu0 = mu0, mu1 = mu1, sigma = sigma, n = n, alpha = alpha,
  sidedness = "greater")
plot_sample_mean_distributions(sampling_example)
```

The one-sided 5% cutoff is $120+1.645\times3=124.935$ mmHg, about 124.93 using the unrounded normal quantile. Here 120 is the null mean, 1.645 is the 95th percentile of the standard normal distribution, and 3 is the standard error. A mean above this cutoff occurs in about 5% of repetitions under the null. At a true mean of 125 mmHg, power is about 51%. Repeating the study at the specified alternative would produce a mean above that threshold about half the time.


```{r errors-app-preview, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_app_preview("alpha_beta", "Move a rejection boundary and explore false positives, false negatives and power.")
```


The shaded error probabilities and power in Figure \@ref(fig:sampling-distribution-figure) are calculated directly from a one-sample normal model with a known population SD.


</details>

## Choosing plausible assumptions {#st01-expectations .advanced-heading}

Your assumptions should explain why previous findings apply to the planned study. Four questions help connect that evidence to the calculation [@cook2018delta2; @cook2019delta2]:

- What would happen with the comparator? Disease severity, background care and follow-up can change the control event percentage or outcome variability. Where data are sparse, expert judgment should be identified and its uncertainty examined.
- What could explain an apparent treatment advantage? In observational comparisons, differences in patients, care or diagnosis can contribute to the observed difference. Earlier diagnosis can lengthen measured survival without postponing death; more detailed staging can change which patients are compared within a disease stage.
- What additional benefit would justify the intervention? Patients and clinicians should consider adverse effects, treatment burden and alternatives when judging a clinically worthwhile difference. More demanding treatment may require a larger benefit to justify its use. The sections on [clinical importance](#what-do-we-expect-what-will-we-plan-for-and-what-matters-clinically) and [ethical review](#ethical-review-and-the-study-protocol) explain how benefit, burden and harm inform this judgment.
- How sensitive is the decision to uncertainty? Plausible ranges should reflect differences between studies and limitations in the evidence. A [sensitivity analysis](#compare-planning-assumptions) shows their implications for required sample size or performance at a fixed count.

The ST01 gastric-cancer surgery trial illustrates these judgments. Its design team used a consensus estimate of 20% five-year survival with conventional (D1) surgery. Apparent advantages of more extensive (D2) surgery in Japanese observational studies could partly reflect earlier diagnosis, more detailed staging, or differences in patients' age and fitness. D2 also carried additional postoperative risks, so the anticipated survival gain needed to justify these harms [@fayers2000beliefs]. The table distinguishes the calculation target from expectations and clinical judgments elicited from 26 surgeons before recruitment.

| Planning role | Reported value and basis |
|:--|:--|
| Anticipated difference | The wider survey anticipated a 9.4-percentage-point survival advantage; the three design-committee surgeons anticipated 13.1 points. |
| Target difference | The detailed calculation used 13.5 points, from 20% to 33.5% survival, giving 400 patients at 90% power. It reflected the design committee's expectations. |
| Clinical importance | The wider survey's average interval of clinical indecision was 4.6–10.8 points. Its upper boundary represented sufficient benefit to favor D2, given the operation's additional risks. Individual judgments varied. |

Table: (\#tab:st01-planning-roles) ST01 planning roles: absolute between-group differences in five-year survival, expressed in percentage points [@fayers2000beliefs].

The survey left the original design unchanged; its clinical boundaries summarize individual surgeons' judgments. Reproducing ST01 requires its survival-analysis method. More generally, differences in patients or care may change the assumed outcomes, while treatment harms inform what benefit is worthwhile. The sample-size consequences depend on those resulting inputs and the chosen analysis.

<span id="planning-uncertainty"></span>

Investigators can overestimate how readily a trial will meet its operational targets. In a prospective survey, investigators assigned an average probability of 78.8% to meeting their recruitment target. Among the 281 trials with evaluable recruitment outcomes, 42.7% met that target. For completing primary data collection on time, the average predicted probability was 72.2%, whereas 13.4% of 536 evaluated trials finished on time. The denominators differ because outcome information was available for different sets of trials. These findings support examining a slower recruitment scenario when using the [screening and enrollment funnel](#recruitment-feasibility) [@benjamin2022forecasts].

<details class="reading-note">
<summary>About the forecast survey</summary>

The survey received responses from 740 principal investigators, a response percentage of 16.7%. Outcome follow-up was incomplete. These features limit how widely its findings can be generalized [@benjamin2022forecasts].

</details>

Uncertainty remains even when assumptions are carefully justified. In a review of 107 randomized trials, the median [standardized treatment effect](#standardized-treatment-effect) used as the calculation target was 0.30, compared with a median observed effect of 0.11 [@rothwell2018targets]. Differences between targets and results can reflect uncertain treatment effects and sampling variability. Assessing investigator optimism also requires evidence about beliefs and their uncertainty before results are known [@liu2024uncertainty].

For your study, earlier observations and elicited expectations can inform a plausible range of population differences. Their values, the target difference and the clinical threshold can coincide or follow a different order. The chosen target needs evidence of plausibility and clinical importance. When a target exceeds the benefit supported by the evidence, your justification should examine power at smaller plausible differences. A [sensitivity analysis](#compare-planning-assumptions) makes these implications visible [@cook2018delta2].

<details class="advanced-explanation" id="further-planning-approaches">
<summary>Planning with uncertainty about the true difference</summary>

Before a diagnostic assessment, symptoms, medical history and the patient population inform how likely a diagnosis seems. A new finding changes that assessment according to how strongly it supports the diagnosis. Bayesian analysis expresses this updating through a [prior](#prior-distribution), the information supplied by new data, and a [posterior](#posterior-distribution).

Consider the neuropathy clinic from [Chapter 4](#estimation-planning). Among 100 comparable patients, 20 have neuropathy. For this teaching example, a test identifies 90% of those with neuropathy and gives a positive result for 10% of those without it. That produces 18 true positives and 8 false positives. Among the 26 positive results, 18 patients have neuropathy: approximately 69%, compared with 20% before testing [@gigerenzer1995frequencies; @binder2021frequencies].

```{r diagnostic-update, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.8, fig.cap="Updating a diagnostic probability using patient counts. The teaching test has 90% sensitivity and 90% specificity. Of 26 positive results, 18 occur in patients with neuropathy, giving a probability of about 69% after a positive result.", fig.alt="A frequency tree starts with 100 clinic patients, of whom 20 have neuropathy. Positive results occur in 18 of these 20 and in 8 of the other 80. The positive-result group therefore contains 18 patients with neuropathy and 8 without it."}
draw_diagnostic_update()
```

The same updating principle can be applied to a treatment difference. Previous evidence informs a prior distribution, and trial results update it. Sample size planning also needs a success criterion: the result that the completed trial must achieve to support its intended conclusion.

The neuropathic pain trial provides a comparison of three approaches. Each uses 56 analyzable patients per group. Standard-treatment relief is assumed to be 30%.

```{r uncertainty-planning-calculations}
# Calculate performance under four possible population differences.
# The helper enumerates possible outcome counts for the Bayesian rule.
uncertain_plan <- neuropathy_uncertain_planning(n = 56)
```

| Approach | Planning question and success criterion |
|:--|:--|
| Frequentist planning with fixed assumptions | If relief is truly 30% with duloxetine and 60% with neravixa, how often will the planned two-sided test give p < 0.05? |
| [Hybrid planning](#hybrid-planning) | Across a stated distribution of possible true differences, how often will that same frequentist test give p < 0.05? |
| [Bayesian planning](#bayesian-planning) | Across possible true differences and future trial data, how often will the posterior probability of a positive treatment difference exceed 97.5%? |

Table: (\#tab:planning-approach-questions) Three planning questions for the same neuropathic pain trial. The Bayesian example specifies a directional benefit criterion.

With a fixed true difference of 30 percentage points, the normal planning approximation gives about 90% power. For hybrid planning, suppose the uncertainty about the population difference is represented by the following four possibilities. These weights are teaching assumptions. A study's weights should be justified using relevant evidence and elicited judgments [@kunzmann2021review; @pezeshk2003].

```{r uncertainty-scenarios, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `True difference (percentage points)` = round(100 * (uncertain_plan$p_novel - .30)),
  `Chance of p < 0.05` = percent(uncertain_plan$fixed_power),
  `Planning weight` = percent(uncertain_plan$weights), check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Illustrative uncertainty distribution and approximate rejection probabilities with 56 patients per group. At a zero difference, rejection is a false positive. At a nonzero difference, the probability is power.")
```

The weighted probability is approximately `r round(100 * uncertain_plan$assurance)`%. This is [assurance](#assurance) for the stated success criterion, p < 0.05: the probability of meeting that criterion averaged over the assumed uncertainty. The 90% power calculation answers the more specific question in which the true difference is fixed at 30 points. A different success criterion, such as evidence of benefit in the positive direction, requires its own calculation.

For the Bayesian analysis, suppose each treatment's relief probability initially has a uniform distribution between 0% and 100%. These independent Beta(1,1) analysis priors allow differences in either direction. Suppose the trial then observes relief in 34 of 56 neravixa patients and 17 of 56 duloxetine patients. Updating the priors gives a posterior probability of a positive treatment difference of `r formatC(100 * uncertain_plan$posterior_benefit, digits=2, format="f")`%, exceeding the specified 97.5% criterion [@fda2010bayesian].

```{r bayesian-update, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.7, fig.cap="The analysis prior and posterior for the population relief difference. Independent uniform priors for the two treatment percentages produce the broad dashed curve. Observing 34 of 56 versus 17 of 56 patients with relief produces the concentrated posterior. Its area to the right of zero is the posterior probability of benefit.", fig.alt="The prior distribution spans treatment differences from minus 100 to 100 percentage points. The posterior after the specified trial data is concentrated near a positive 30-point difference, with almost all its area above zero."}
draw_bayesian_update()
```

Before observing data, the probability of meeting this Bayesian criterion is approximately `r round(100 * uncertain_plan$bayes_assurance)`% under the same four planning scenarios. The calculation evaluates every possible pair of event counts and weights them by their binomial probabilities. The four-scenario planning distribution describes which true outcomes are considered plausible when designing the trial. The analysis priors define how the eventual data update the evidence. Both choices, the success criterion and sensitivity to other priors belong in the report. Operating characteristics, including false positives under no effect, should be checked [@fda2010bayesian].

The [commented calculation](#uncertainty-calculation-details) records the procedures. Safeguard power is another approach that incorporates uncertainty in a previous effect estimate [@perugini2014]. A review of Bayesian randomized trials found hybrid planning common and fully Bayesian sample size methods rarely used [@marks2026].

</details>


```{r consider-plausible-assumptions, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_consider_check("consider-plausible-assumptions")
```

## Sensitivity to other assumptions {#stress-test-the-study-plan .advanced-heading}

<span id="compare-planning-assumptions"></span>
<span id="tab:pain-core-sensitivity"></span>

A [sensitivity analysis](#sensitivity-analysis){.no-glossary-tooltip} examines what happens when a planning assumption changes within a plausible range. The earlier curves varied the true treatment difference. Figure \@ref(fig:assumption-sensitivity) now keeps that difference fixed and examines two other inputs.

Suppose the earlier evidence may overstate relief with standard treatment. Keep 100 analyzable patients per group and a true difference of 20 percentage points. Compare relief probabilities of 10% versus 30%, 30% versus 50%, and 50% versus 70%. The difference is unchanged, but the variability of binary outcomes changes. The left panel of Figure \@ref(fig:assumption-sensitivity) shows the consequence for power.

The right panel asks a second question for a continuous outcome: what if individual scores vary more than expected? It keeps the mean difference at 3 units and increases the common SD. Read the power change first, then use Table \@ref(tab:pain-target-sensitivity) to find the sample needed to recover 90% power. Each comparison changes one planning assumption and leads to a concrete recruitment or design decision.

```{r assumption-sensitivity, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="Sensitivity at 100 analyzable patients per group and a two-sided Type I error probability of 5%. Left: the between-group relief difference stays at 20 percentage points while standard-treatment relief varies. Right: the mean difference stays at 3 units while the common standard deviation varies. Dots mark standard-treatment relief of 30% and SD 5; dashed lines mark 90% target power.", fig.alt="Two panels use power from 0 to 100 percent vertically. The left varies standard-treatment relief from 10 to 60 percent, adding 20 points for novel treatment; power changes with the event probabilities. The right varies the common SD from 4 to 9 at a mean difference of 3; power falls as variability increases."}
# Hold both sample sizes and treatment differences fixed.
binary_curve_spec <- curve_spec
binary_curve_spec$p_treatment <- .50
mean_curve_spec <- study_spec(outcome = "means", n = analyzable_cap,
  delta = 3, sd = 5)
draw_assumption_sensitivity(binary_curve_spec, mean_curve_spec, target_power)
```

<span id="fig:pain-target-sensitivity-plot"></span>

```{r pain-target-sensitivity, echo=FALSE}
baseline_scenarios <- lapply(c(.10, .30, .50), function(p) {
  x <- binary_curve_spec; x$p_control <- p; x$p_treatment <- p + .20; x
})
sd_scenarios <- lapply(c(5, 7, 9), function(sd) {
  x <- mean_curve_spec; x$sd <- sd; x
})
alternatives <- c(baseline_scenarios, sd_scenarios)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Assumption = c("Relief: standard 10%, novel 30%", "Relief: standard 30%, novel 50%",
    "Relief: standard 50%, novel 70%", "Mean difference 3; SD 5",
    "Mean difference 3; SD 7", "Mean difference 3; SD 9"),
  `Power with 100 per group` = percent(vapply(alternatives, spec_power, numeric(1))),
  `Patients per group for 90% power` = vapply(alternatives,
    function(x) plan_n(x, target_power = target_power), numeric(1)),
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Sensitivity to event probabilities and outcome variability. The mean comparison uses a pooled two-sample t-test calculation.")
```

<span id="tab:fixed-plan-sensitivity"></span>

For binary outcomes, the event probabilities determine variability, so the same absolute difference can give different power. For continuous outcomes, a larger standard deviation makes the specified mean difference harder to detect. Relevant evidence should support the alternatives and their ranges [@cook2018delta2; @candel2023].

The [Sample size reasoning lab](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/book/curves.html#activity-pain_curves) lets you vary the event percentages, mean difference, standard deviation and available sample used in the sensitivity analysis. Its Description explains how the calculated curves and simulated studies relate. Your sample size calculation report should record the alternatives that affect the decision. For example, the BEP protocol presents its principal calculation in the main text and alternative assumptions in an additional file [@wang2024bep]. DELTA² and CONSORT recommend documenting sensitivity to calculation inputs [@cook2018delta2; @consortee2025].

## When the available sample is insufficient {#what-if-the-study-is-too-small-for-its-purpose .advanced-heading}

### Underpowered studies {#underpowered-studies .advanced-heading}

An underpowered study has a low probability of obtaining a statistically significant result when the specified difference is present in the population. For the neuropathic pain trial with 100 patients per group, power is about 59% if the true difference is 15 percentage points. Across repeated trials under these assumptions, approximately 41% would fail to detect that difference.

In underpowered studies, sampling variability can be large relative to the treatment difference. Studies that obtain statistically significant results favoring treatment tend to have unusually large estimates of its benefit. Focusing on those significant results can therefore exaggerate the apparent benefit [@gelman2014beyond]. This concerns selection of unusually large estimates. Whether an estimated benefit is worthwhile requires the separate comparison with the clinical threshold, treatment harms and burden.

Larger samples reduce [sampling variability](#sampling-variability). Addressing bias requires attention to the design, measurement and analysis.


```{r consider-exaggerated-benefit, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_consider_check("consider-exaggerated-benefit")
```

### Ways to increase power {#increase-power .advanced-heading}

Before collecting data, you can consider whether the design could provide more information about the treatment effect. Table \@ref(tab:increase-power) summarizes changes to recruitment, measurement and analysis.

Power can improve through more informative measurements, appropriate use of baseline information, and a design that makes efficient treatment comparisons. Which changes help depends on the outcome, allocation and planned analysis. Prespecified adjustment for baseline variables that predict the outcome can improve precision and power in a randomized trial. For example, patients with more severe baseline pain may also have higher follow-up scores. Including baseline pain in the analysis can explain some of this variation, allowing a more precise treatment comparison. Confounding in an observational comparison requires its own design and analysis justification. Covariate adjustment can improve efficiency for binary, ordinal and time-to-event outcomes as well as continuous outcomes [@fda2023covariates]. The continuous-outcome calculations in @candel2023 illustrate the roles of allocation, baseline information and within-person comparisons.

| Option | Why it can help | What to consider |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Increase the analyzable sample | More independent patients reduce sampling variability at the same true difference. | Another center or a longer recruitment period could supply more patients. [Multicenter planning](#multicenter-trials) should reflect allocation within centers and the intended analysis. |
| Improve follow-up and outcome completeness | More recorded outcomes preserve the analyzable sample. | Accessible follow-up and reminders can help. Reasons for missing outcomes inform the missing-data analysis. |
| Improve measurement | Reliable measurements reduce noise and support more informative comparisons. | A consistent definition and assessment time matter for pain relief. A different outcome needs its own calculation. |
| Use an efficient design and analysis | Informative baseline measurements or appropriate paired comparisons can improve precision and power. | Adjustment should be prespecified. A [crossover trial](#crossover-trial) requires suitable treatment reversibility, disease stability and control of carryover. |
| Keep allocation balanced when appropriate | With equal variances, equal group sizes efficiently use a fixed total for a two-means comparison. | Other outcome distributions or design requirements can justify a different allocation and matching calculation. |

Table: (\#tab:increase-power) Design changes that can improve power and their planning implications.

Changing the Type I error probability or using a one-sided test changes the rejection rule. A higher Type I error probability increases both power and false-positive probability. A one-sided test concentrates rejection in a prespecified direction. These choices need scientific justification before data collection [@moye2002].

<span id="model-answer-larger-study-resources"></span>

### Decisions with a fixed sample {#available-sample .advanced-heading}

The neuropathic pain example provides 100 analyzable patients per group. It exceeds the 90% power target at a 30-point difference, but power at the clinically important 20-point difference is about 83%. If 90% power at 20 points is essential, the calculation requires 124 analyzable patients per group. The [Sample size reasoning lab](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/book/curves.html#activity-pain_curves) lets you examine how changing the available count affects that conclusion.

Your justification should state the available sample, the plausible assumptions and the power they imply. The next decision is whether additional recruitment or a scientifically appropriate design change is feasible. A revised research objective should be agreed before data collection and supported by its own calculation.

<span id="a-fixed-total-of-70-patients"></span>
<span id="sensitivity-is-not-observed-post-hoc-power"></span>

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-observed-power">
<summary>Common misconception: the observed treatment difference can tell me how much power my completed trial had</summary>

A trial may observe a large difference partly because of sampling variability. Entering that result into a power calculation simply restates information already reflected in its p value. The estimate and confidence interval describe the result. To assess the design, power can be calculated at independently justified differences, such as the prespecified 20- and 30-point benefits [@consortee2025; @lakens2022].

</details>

<div class="chapter-recap">

### Take-home points {.unnumbered}

- Power at one true difference and assurance across uncertain assumptions answer different planning questions. A success criterion specifies the result the study needs to achieve.
- The vertical reference line gives power at the available sample. The horizontal line gives the sample required for the selected power target. Comparing both supports a justified recruitment or design decision.
- Relevant evidence and its uncertainty should support the plausible assumptions examined.
- Event probabilities and outcome variability affect power even when the treatment difference stays fixed.
- When power is insufficient, the planning decision concerns feasible recruitment, design changes or a justified revision of the objective.

</div>

render_chapter_quiz("curves")
