# Building and evaluating simulations {#simulation .advanced-heading}


::: {.learning-goals .advanced-outcomes}
After this chapter, you should be able to:

- Generate and analyze one hypothetical trial.
- Repeat the trial to assess rejection and interval coverage.
- Explain how [Monte Carlo uncertainty](#monte-carlo-error) differs from uncertainty in the planning assumptions.
- Compare simulated performance with a planning approximation.
- Assess how unavailable outcomes and selective losses affect estimates and coverage.
- Describe how evaluating interim decisions and adaptations extends the simulation workflow.
:::

Suppose the neuropathic pain trial enrolls 100 analyzable patients per group, with population relief probabilities of 60% and 30%. A [simulation](#statistical-simulation) runs this experiment entirely on a computer, generating patient outcomes and analyzing each trial. Repeating the experiment produces different results under the same population assumptions. This chapter follows one trial through its analysis, then uses many trials to assess power and simulation uncertainty. Further examples examine missing outcomes and interim decisions.

Simulation is useful when the planned analysis or dependence between observations makes a simple formula inadequate. A simulation study should specify its aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands (quantities to estimate), methods and performance measures—the ADEMP framework [@morris2019; @pargent2024]. Here these are the relief probabilities, between-group difference, score test and confidence interval, and their performance across repeated trials.

The examples use R. The inline activity can run the supplied scenarios in the browser. Its downloads include an R script and inputs for running or modifying them from a repository checkout. The [practical reproduction steps in Chapter 8](#reproduce-or-adapt-the-examples) explain how to restore the environment and run that script.

## Generating and analyzing repeated trials {#activity-3-generate-analyze-repeat-summarize .advanced-heading}

Start with the study that is being planned: define its population, patient count and intended analysis, then generate outcomes under those assumptions [@superpowerbook2022; @morris2019]. The binary example uses the same score test as the [existing reasoning lab](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/book/simulation.html#activity-pain_simulation).


```{r simulation-app-preview, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_app_preview("pain_simulation", "Generate patient outcomes and examine results across repeated trials.")
```


This extends the core simulation: the question is now whether the analysis has useful power, confidence interval coverage and interval width under the specified population. The activity opens in *Repeated trials*. You can first select *One trial* to follow one generated dataset through its analysis, then return to *Repeated trials* and run 5,000 repetitions. Each trial contains 100 patients per group; the simulation repeats that trial 5,000 times.

Figure \@ref(fig:simulation-loop) shows how these repetitions surround the generation and analysis of one trial. The population assumptions and analysis stay fixed while each repetition generates new patient outcomes.

```{r simulation-loop, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=5.2, fig.cap="The simulation repeats a complete trial and its analysis 5,000 times. Each trial contains 100 patients per group. Changing the patients per group changes the study design; increasing the repetitions improves the precision of the estimated simulation performance.", fig.alt="A loop connects four steps. Generate one trial with 100 patients per group under standard and novel relief probabilities of 30% and 60%. Analyze its difference, confidence interval and p-value. Repeat generation and analysis for 5,000 independent trials. Summarize power, confidence interval coverage and width across those trials."}
draw_simulation_loop()
```

### Step 1: generate one trial {.advanced-heading}

This simulation uses 100 independent patients per group, with relief probabilities of 30% and 60%. The basic planning calculation gave 56 per group; 100 is the available analyzable count examined in Chapter 5 and used here to evaluate the same design. The true population difference assumed in this simulation is the 30-percentage-point [target difference](#target-difference). Each patient's outcome is zero (no relief) or one (relief).

```{r generate-trial}
# Fix the random-number starting point so rerunning this code reproduces the trial.
set.seed(20260921)
n <- 100
# Generate one 0/1 outcome per patient: 1 = relief, 0 = no relief.
control <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = .30)
treatment <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = .60)
# sum() counts the patients with relief in each group.
c(control_relief = sum(control), treatment_relief = sum(treatment))
```

```{r generate-trial-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Group=c("Standard treatment", "Novel treatment"), Patients=n, `Reporting relief`=c(sum(control),sum(treatment)), `Relief percentage`=percent(c(mean(control),mean(treatment))), check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Observed pain relief in one simulated trial.")
```

### Step 2: apply the planned analysis {.advanced-heading}

Each simulated trial is analyzed using a two-sided pooled [score test](#score-test) without continuity correction. The helper also calculates a Newcombe-Wilson interval for the risk difference [@newcombe1998]. The score test evaluates zero difference using a pooled estimate of the event probability under that null. The Newcombe–Wilson interval combines Wilson limits for the two separate proportions. It is not obtained by inverting this pooled test, so rejection and interval exclusion of zero can occasionally disagree near the decision boundary. Record the named test and interval procedure, as shown in the [methods table](#tutorial-methods).

```{r analyze-trial}
# Analyze the relief counts using the tutorial's binary-outcome helper.
# The returned result includes the difference, confidence interval and p-value.
one_result <- analyse_binary(sum(treatment), sum(control), n, alpha = .05)
one_result
```

```{r analyze-trial-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Measure=c("Observed treatment difference", "95% confidence interval", "p-value", "Testing decision"), Result=c(paste(round(100*one_result$estimate,1),"percentage points"), paste(round(100*one_result$lower,1),"to",round(100*one_result$upper,1),"percentage points"), formatC(one_result$p_value,format="f",digits=3), if(one_result$p_value < .05) "Reject the zero-difference null" else "Do not reject the zero-difference null")),
  caption = "Estimated benefit and testing decision in one simulated trial.")
```

`estimate` is treatment minus control; `lower` and `upper` are confidence limits. The [p-value](#p-value) tests a zero difference. The helper's score-test p-value can be checked against R:

```{r independent-check}
# Check the helper against R's two-sided test of independent proportions.
# Group sizes are supplied twice; no continuity correction is applied.
reference <- prop.test(c(sum(treatment), sum(control)), c(n, n),
  correct = FALSE)
# Compare the two p-values; $ selects a named component of each result.
c(helper_p = one_result$p_value, R_p = reference$p.value)
```

```{r independent-check-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Method=c("Tutorial helper", "R score test"), `p-value`=formatC(c(one_result$p_value,reference$p.value),format="f",digits=4), check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Agreement between two implementations of the planned score test.")
```

This comparison checks agreement between the p-value calculations. The two functions use different confidence-interval methods. When both groups have all successes or all failures, the helper returns a p-value of one.

### Step 3: repeat independent trials {.advanced-heading}

The efficient helper generates the event count in each group directly from a binomial distribution. This is equivalent to adding up independent binary outcomes in each group. It applies the same analysis to every trial.

```{r repeat-trials}
# Specify one trial's assumptions and B = 5,000 independent repetitions.
trial_spec <- study_spec(outcome = "proportions", n = 100,
  p_control = .30, p_treatment = .60, alpha = .05,
  threshold = .20, width_target = .30, B = 5000, seed = 20260921)
# Generate and analyze all trials using the same assumptions.
trials <- simulate_trials(trial_spec)
# Display only the first four rows of the results.
head(trials$results, 4)
```

### Step 4: summarize what the design achieves {.advanced-heading}

```{r trial-summary}
# Summarize results across trials, including Monte Carlo uncertainty.
# Format the summary as a table.
knitr::kable(display_simulation_summary(simulation_summary(trials)),
  caption = "Performance across repeated studies, with Monte Carlo standard errors and 95% intervals.")
```

The percentage of statistically significant simulated results estimates [power](#statistical-power) under these assumptions. Coverage is the percentage of [confidence intervals](#confidence-interval) containing the true population difference assumed in the simulation. The percentage meeting the width target counts intervals with a full width no greater than 30 [percentage points](#percentage-points). Full width is the upper limit minus the lower limit. An interval from 12 to 38 percentage points has width $38-12=26$ points and meets that target. Power, coverage and width attainment describe three separate properties.


```{r consider-coverage, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_consider_check("consider-coverage")
```

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-simulation-repetitions">
<summary>Common misconception: running 5,000 simulations gives each trial more power than running 20</summary>

With 20 patients per group in every trial, adding simulations gives a more stable estimate of how often that design detects a difference. As thousands of trials accumulate, the detected fraction tends toward the power of the simulated test. Increasing the patients per group changes the information available within each trial and can increase its power.

</details>

```{r trial-intervals, echo=FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Risk-difference confidence intervals from the first 30 simulated trials. Filled dots indicate rejection of zero. Reference lines mark the 20-percentage-point clinical threshold and the 30-percentage-point assumed population difference used for planning.", fig.alt="Intervals vary from trial to trial. Separate lines mark zero, the 20-point clinical threshold and the 30-point assumed population difference. The preceding table reports rejection, coverage and attainment of the full interval width target across all 5,000 trials."}
plot_trial_intervals(trials$results, trial_spec)
```

<details class="advanced-explanation" id="sample-size-simulation-distributions">
<summary>Comparing results at different sample sizes</summary>

The core activity generated 5,000 trials at each of 20, 50 and 80 patients per group, assuming 30% and 60% relief. Returning to those trials, the following histograms count the two-sided [p-values](#p-value) from the independent simulated trials. Both positive and negative differences can produce small p values. The dashed line marks the chosen significance level. The fraction below the line estimates power under the specified alternative (Figure \@ref(fig:p-values)).

```{r p-values, echo=FALSE, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Two-sided p values from 5,000 independent clinical trials at each sample size. The percentage of p-values below the chosen significance level estimates power for the assumed relief probabilities.", fig.alt="Three histograms compare two-sided p values with 20, 50 and 80 patients per group. The percentages of statistically significant results and their Monte Carlo intervals are in the following table."}
par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (batch in batches) plot_p_values(batch)
```

```{r simulation-monte-carlo-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `Patients per group` = power_results$n_per_group,
  `Total patients` = power_results$total,
  `Simulated trials` = power_results$replications,
  `Estimated power` = percent(power_results$simulated_power),
  `95% Monte Carlo lower limit` = percent(power_results$MC_lower_95),
  `95% Monte Carlo upper limit` = percent(power_results$MC_upper_95), check.names=FALSE),
  row.names=FALSE, caption = "Estimated power and Monte Carlo intervals for the three simulated sample sizes.")
```


</details>

## Precision of a simulation {#precision-of-a-simulation .advanced-heading}

Even with unchanged assumptions, another batch of simulated trials will give a slightly different estimated power. This is [Monte Carlo error](#monte-carlo-error){.no-glossary-tooltip}: uncertainty caused by using a finite number of simulation repetitions. More repetitions reduce Monte Carlo uncertainty while the number of patients in each trial stays fixed.


The rejection fraction estimates power under a specified nonzero difference, or false-positive probability under a zero difference. Both estimates have Monte Carlo uncertainty.

A treatment-effect interval describes uncertainty in one trial estimate. A Monte Carlo interval describes uncertainty in a performance estimate obtained from a finite number of simulated trials. Keeping the trial size fixed and increasing repetitions improves the latter.

Here, $n$ denotes patients per group and $B$ denotes the number of simulated studies. If $\hat p$ is the simulated rejection fraction, its approximate Monte Carlo standard error is:

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{MCSE}=\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/B}.
(\#eq:mcse)
\end{equation}

If 4,000 of 5,000 simulated studies give statistically significant results, estimated power is 80%. Its MCSE is about `r round(100 * sqrt(.8 * .2 / 5000), 2)` percentage points. The tables use Wilson intervals for Monte Carlo uncertainty. These intervals remain informative even when a simulation observes no rejections or all rejections. With a similar rejection fraction, MCSE is proportional to $1/\sqrt B$. Four times as many repetitions approximately halves it. Increasing 5,000 repetitions to 20,000 reduces the MCSE from about 0.57 to 0.28 percentage points at 80% power. This improves numerical precision for the specified scenario. Uncertainty about the real treatment effect is assessed by varying the population assumptions.

## Compare simulation with a planning approximation {.advanced-heading}

```{r simulation-benchmark}
# TRUE/FALSE rejection indicators have a mean equal to the fraction rejecting.
# Compare that simulated power with the normal planning approximation.
c(simulated_power = mean(trials$results$reject),
  approximate_planning_power = spec_power(trial_spec))
```

```{r simulation-benchmark-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Method=c("Repeated-trial simulation", "Planning approximation"), Power=percent(c(mean(trials$results$reject),spec_power(trial_spec)))),
  caption = "Power estimated by simulation and by the planning approximation.")
```

A difference can reflect Monte Carlo error or the approximation used for binary planning. Increasing the number of simulations reduces only the Monte Carlo component. Simulation evaluates the analysis under specified assumptions. Their suitability for the clinical study requires supporting evidence.


```{r consider-simulation-agreement, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_consider_check("consider-simulation-agreement")
```



## Explore missing outcomes {#explore-missing-outcomes .advanced-heading}

The percentage of participants lost to follow-up may differ between treatment groups. This is called *differential dropout*. For example, outcomes might be missing for 20% of participants receiving the novel treatment and 10% receiving standard treatment. When such differences are anticipated, sample size planning should account for the expected retention in each group and the planned allocation ratio. A single overall dropout percentage can conceal a shortfall in one group.

The reasons for missing outcomes also matter. In the neuropathic pain trial, patients who experience little relief might be more likely to miss the final assessment. If this happens more often in the novel-treatment group, an analysis restricted to participants with observed outcomes could overestimate its benefit. [Bias](#bias) can occur with equal or unequal dropout percentages. Assessing it requires information about why outcomes are missing, the treatment effect being estimated, and the analysis used [@bell2013dropout].

Your sample size calculation report should describe how missing outcomes will be minimized, how their reasons will be recorded in each group, and how the analysis will handle them. [Sensitivity analyses](#sensitivity-analysis) should examine whether conclusions change under plausible alternative assumptions about the missing outcomes [@little2012missing].

The simulations below start with recruited participants so that losses affect the number available for analysis.

The [repeated neuropathic pain trial activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/book/simulation.html#activity-pain_simulation) also lets you examine how missing outcomes affect a treatment comparison. In *Settings*, the *Explore missing outcomes* controls offer four scenarios. Each uses the same recruited count and the same population relief probabilities, so you can distinguish the consequences of losing information from those of selectively losing particular outcomes.

| Scenario | Assumptions about missing outcomes |
|:--|:--|
| Complete outcomes | Every recruited participant has an observed outcome. |
| Equal losses | 10% expected loss in each group, unrelated to relief. |
| Unequal losses | 10% expected loss with standard treatment and 20% with novel treatment, unrelated to relief. |
| Outcome-related losses | The same overall expected losses of 10% and 20%; in the novel-treatment group, participants without relief are three times as likely to have missing outcomes as those with relief. |

Table: Missing-outcome scenarios in the repeated neuropathic pain trial activity.

This [sensitivity analysis](#sensitivity-analysis) uses hypothetical teaching assumptions. In the outcome-related scenario, the missingness probabilities are calibrated to preserve 20% expected loss in the novel-treatment group. At 60% population relief, the probabilities of a missing outcome are approximately 11.1% among those with relief and 33.3% among those without it. Actual losses vary between simulated studies. Equal recruitment is retained; group sizes after loss can differ.

In *One trial*, you can see recruited, retained, and missing counts in each group, together with example participant records. The simulation shows the underlying outcomes for teaching, including those marked missing. The analysis uses only observed outcomes. In a real study, those missing outcomes would be unknown.

In *Repeated trials*, the mean estimated difference is compared with the known population difference; their difference estimates bias. Coverage is assessed against that same full-population difference. The table also reports retained counts, interval widths, and statistically significant results. A high significance percentage can accompany biased estimates and poor coverage. Comparisons with no observed outcomes in one group are reported as unavailable; performance summaries use the estimable comparisons.

The available-case analysis uses a two-sided pooled score test and a Newcombe-Wilson interval with the actual retained group sizes. It illustrates the consequences of a simple analysis under different missingness assumptions. Planning an appropriate missing-data analysis for a real trial requires assumptions and methods matched to the intended treatment effect [@bell2013dropout; @little2012missing]. The [recruitment discussion](#account-for-expected-losses) explains differential dropout and recruitment allowances; the [methods section](#tutorial-methods) records the simulation procedures.


```{r consider-missing-outcomes, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_consider_check("consider-missing-outcomes")
```



## How the simulations work {#simulation-reproducibility .advanced-heading}

<details class="advanced-explanation">
<summary>How the simulations work</summary>

The preceding sections explain what the simulation evaluates. The following implementation details identify how the apps generate data and record results so that a saved batch can be reproduced.

For one binary trial, the app generates independent Bernoulli patient outcomes. For repeated trials, it generates binomial event counts for each group and analyzes each pair of counts. The animation and batch summaries use these same counts, estimated differences and p values. The individual records in a repeated-trial report represent the first trial in its batch. Normal-outcome studies assume independent observations with a common SD. The repeated-study implementation generates normally distributed mean differences and chi-squared pooled variances; under these assumptions, these have the same sampling distributions as the corresponding summaries of complete patient datasets.

Simulation summaries should retain the number of repetitions, Monte Carlo standard error and interval procedure. The apps use Wilson intervals for simulated rejection and coverage fractions.

The missing-outcome extension uses binary relief outcomes and a fixed recruited count per group. Its four scenarios assume no loss, 10% loss in both groups, 10%/20% loss independent of relief, or 10%/20% loss with outcome-related selection in the novel-treatment group. For population relief probability $p$, overall loss $r$, and missingness risk ratio $k$ for no relief versus relief, the probabilities are $q_{\mathrm{relief}}=r/[p+k(1-p)]$ and $q_{\mathrm{no\ relief}}=kq_{\mathrm{relief}}$. The selective scenario uses $k=3$ in the novel group and $k=1$ in the standard group. One trial generates patient outcomes and missingness indicators; repeated studies use mathematically equivalent multinomial counts for observed/missing outcomes with/without relief. Available cases are analyzed using the actual group sizes, the pooled score test without continuity correction, and Newcombe-Wilson intervals. Bias and coverage refer to the full recruited population difference. Unestimable comparisons are counted separately. Downloads record the scenario, recruitment count, loss assumptions, selection multiplier, population probabilities, repetition count, and random seed.

The random seed, random-number generator settings and software environment help reproduce a particular simulated batch. Changing the simulation algorithm can change the realized random draws even when its statistical model is equivalent. Agreement of individual random outcomes requires the same computational procedure as well as the same assumptions.

</details>

## Simulating interim decisions and adaptations {#simulating-decision-rules .advanced-heading}

The neuropathic pain simulations in this chapter each use one final analysis. A design with [interim analyses or stopping guidelines](#interim-analyses-stopping) needs each simulated trial to follow its complete decision process: generate the data available at the first planned analysis, apply the relevant rule, then stop or continue. If [sample-size re-estimation](#sample-size-re-estimation) is planned, the simulation should apply that rule and the corresponding final analysis [@fdaadaptive2019].

An [interim futility rule](#futility) specifies when accumulating evidence gives too little prospect of meeting the planned success criterion to justify continuing. For example, a prespecified rule might stop recruitment if a calculated conditional probability of eventual success falls below a chosen threshold. That rule and its assumptions need evaluation with the final analysis.

The evaluation should include scenarios with no treatment difference to estimate false-positive probability, and plausible beneficial differences to estimate power. With [several confirmatory claims](#multiple-outcomes-comparisons), it should also consider scenarios where some null hypotheses are true and others are false. Useful summaries include the probability of stopping at each stage, the expected sample size and its distribution, and the accuracy of effect estimates and confidence intervals. These are operating characteristics: how the complete design would behave if many trials were conducted under the same assumptions [@iche91998; @fdaadaptive2019].

For example, a proposed interim look in the neuropathic pain trial would require a simulation that includes four-week outcome availability, the stopping boundary and any recruitment already underway when a decision is made. The current [neuropathic pain simulation activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/book/simulation.html#activity-pain_simulation) illustrates the fixed-sample workflow. Evaluating interim decisions requires a design-specific implementation with a statistician and the [additional reporting record](#complex-design-record).

## Evaluating the discharge calculation {#discharge-simulation .advanced-heading}

The [discharge exercise](#discharge) compares standard care at 80% with treatment at 96% or 90%, using target power of 80% or 90%. Outcomes near 100% leave few patients without the event, so the test approximation deserves closer examination.

The [discharge simulation activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/power_explorer/?activity=discharge) estimates the specified test's rejection probability at the calculated sample size. A null scenario also checks false-positive probability near the 100% boundary. The discharge example compares simulated rejection percentages with calculated power, applying the [simulation evaluation approach](#precision-of-a-simulation) near a boundary of the event probability.


<div class="chapter-recap">

### Take-home points {.unnumbered}

- Simulation generates data, applies the planned analysis, and summarizes repeated results.
- Simulated power and coverage depend on the assumed population and analysis.
- Monte Carlo uncertainty quantifies finite-simulation error; checking the analysis also requires comparing methods and assumptions.
- Missing outcomes can reduce information, and selective missingness can bias estimates even with additional recruitment.
- Evaluating an adaptive design requires simulating its complete decision rules, including when it stops and how it changes sample size.

</div>

# Reproducibility and open science {#appendix .advanced-heading}

::: {.learning-goals .advanced-outcomes}
After this chapter, you should be able to:

- Explain how computational reproducibility, replication and open science support scrutiny of research.
- Validate a sample size calculation using a second implementation, expected input–output relationships and documented settings.
- Specify the protocol, SAP, software and amendment records needed to check a calculation.
- Reproduce a saved result and document changes when adapting it to another study.
:::

Another researcher should be able to rerun the neuropathic pain calculation and recover 56 analyzable patients and 59 recruits per group. That requires the inputs, procedure, software and rounding decisions recorded in the [calculation report](#sample-size-report-methods). This chapter explains how to preserve and share that record, compare software and reproduce a saved calculation. The detailed simulation algorithms are in [Chapter 6](#simulation-reproducibility).

## Why reproducibility matters {#why-reproducibility-matters .advanced-heading}

A sample-size result is useful when another researcher can understand how it was obtained, check the calculation, and assess whether its assumptions fit the proposed study. Numerical inputs, statistical procedures, software settings and rounding rules can all affect the result. Clear documentation makes errors easier to identify and allows you to revisit the plan when new evidence becomes available.

Here, computational reproducibility means obtaining consistent results using the same inputs, computational procedures and conditions. Replicability concerns whether studies collecting new data to address the same scientific question produce consistent findings. These definitions follow @nas2019. Reproducing a calculation helps establish that its implementation can be checked. Its assumptions and the suitability of the study design still require scientific judgment.

Open science supports scrutiny and reuse by making research methods, outputs and supporting resources accessible. A shared protocol, analysis code, documented assumptions and an identified software version help others understand and build on your work. Data access should respect consent, confidentiality and other legitimate restrictions [@unesco2021]. The synthetic examples here allow you to explore and share the computational workflow without using patient records.


```{r consider-open-calculation, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_consider_check("consider-open-calculation")
```

## Software and statistical support {#software-support .advanced-heading}

For straightforward calculations, such as comparing two independent group means or percentages, established software can help you calculate sample size and explore alternative assumptions. Your choice should reflect the study design, planned analysis, and inputs you can justify. Table \@ref(tab:software-options) summarizes options with different combinations of calculations, explanations, and graphical displays.

<details id="software-options">
<summary>Software options</summary>

| Resource | Access | Main use |
|:--|:--|:--|
| [R](https://www.r-project.org/) | Free | Scripted calculations and simulations, including the commented examples in this tutorial. Shared inputs and code make repeated checking and adaptation practical. |
| [G\*Power](https://www.psychologie.hhu.de/arbeitsgruppen/allgemeine-psychologie-und-arbeitspsychologie/gpower), [WebPower](https://webpower.psychstat.org/wiki/models/index), and [PAMLj for jamovi](https://pamlj.github.io/) | Free | Power and sample-size calculations for common statistical analyses; the available procedures differ between programs. |
| [Superpower](https://aaroncaldwell.us/SuperpowerBook/) | Free | Planning factorial experiments using means, SDs, and correlations, with simulations and accompanying explanations [@lakenscaldwell2021]. |
| [presize](https://github.com/dcr-unibe-ch/presize) | Free | Planning sample size around the desired width of a confidence interval. |
| [PASS](https://www.ncss.com/software/pass/) | Paid | Dedicated software covering a broad range of power and precision calculations, with documentation of procedures, assumptions, and worked examples [@pass2022]. |
| [nQuery](https://www.statsols.com/) | Paid | Dedicated clinical-trial planning software, including fixed, adaptive, and Bayesian designs; availability depends on the edition. |
| [Stata](https://www.stata.com/features/overview/power-and-sample-size/), [SAS](https://support.sas.com/documentation/cdl/en/statug/66103/HTML/default/statug_power_overview.htm), and [IBM SPSS Statistics](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/spss-statistics/30.0.0?topic=features-power-analysis) | Licensed statistical software | Power and sample-size procedures within an analysis environment your institution may already provide. |

Table: (\#tab:software-options) Selected software for power, sample-size, and precision planning. Available procedures depend on the program, version, and edition.

</details>

Begin with the procedure needed for the study and the software supported by the course, institution or statistical adviser. For a standard calculation, a documented graphical tool may be convenient. Scripted work in R can support repeated scenarios and simulations. Specialized trial designs may need dedicated software or code. A local course can specify its required tool. The table supports selecting a suitable route without requiring students to learn every listed program.

The documentation for the version you use should identify the procedure and its assumptions. Your report should record that version and the selected settings so the calculation can be checked.

Real studies often involve additional decisions. Early consultation with a statistician is especially useful when:

- observations are related, as in repeated measurements, crossover studies, or participants grouped within clinics;
- the study involves several primary outcomes, multiple comparisons, interim analyses, or non-inferiority or equivalence objectives;
- the target difference or variability is uncertain, recruitment is limited, or missing outcomes and treatment switching may affect the analysis.

Involving a statistician while the research question and protocol are still being developed can help you choose a suitable design and analysis, justify the planning assumptions, and identify information you need to collect. These decisions can prevent avoidable changes later. Clinical-trial guidance emphasizes statistical collaboration, documentation of assumptions, and investigation of their consequences [@iche91998; @cook2018delta2]. The example below illustrates why the meaning of a software input deserves the same attention as its numerical value.

### Beware of your assumptions in every calculation tool or software you use {#gpower-assumptions .advanced-heading}

Every calculation depends on the selected method and the meaning of its inputs. The [continuous-outcome example](#two-means) illustrates this using G\*Power. The target difference between group means is 3 score units, the common within-group SD is 5, allocation is equal, the two-sided Type I error probability is 5%, and target power is 90%.

[G\*Power](https://www.psychologie.hhu.de/arbeitsgruppen/allgemeine-psychologie-und-arbeitspsychologie/gpower) asks for different effect-size measures depending on the selected analysis [@faul2007]. For an independent-samples t test, Cohen's $d$ expresses the target difference relative to the common within-group SD:

\begin{equation}
d=\frac{3}{5}=0.60.
(\#eq:standardized-d)
\end{equation}

The one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) procedure asks for Cohen's $f$. It describes the spread of the group means around their overall mean, relative to the within-group SD. With two equally sized groups, a common SD and no covariate adjustment, the group means each lie half the between-group difference from their overall mean. Consequently [@gpowermanual2023]:

\begin{equation}
f=\frac{d}{2}=\frac{0.60}{2}=0.30.
(\#eq:standardized-f)
\end{equation}

The letter beside the effect-size field changes which value you should enter. Table \@ref(tab:gpower-effect-sizes) shows the consequence of entering $d$ in a field that expects $f$.

```{r gpower-calculation}
# Store the same mean difference, SD and statistical criteria in one list.
gpower_inputs <- list(difference = 3, sd = 5, alpha = .05, power = .90)
# Standardize the difference. For two equally sized groups only, f = d / 2.
gpower_d <- gpower_inputs$difference / gpower_inputs$sd
gpower_f <- gpower_d / 2
# Obtain the independent two-sample t-test requirement as a reference.
gpower_t_plan <- stats::power.t.test(
  delta = gpower_inputs$difference, sd = gpower_inputs$sd,
  sig.level = gpower_inputs$alpha, power = gpower_inputs$power,
  type = "two.sample", alternative = "two.sided", strict = TRUE)
# Calculate one-way ANOVA power for two equally sized groups.
# qf() finds the null cutoff; pf() gives the probability beyond it under the alternative.
anova_power <- function(n_per_group, f) {
  df_error <- 2 * n_per_group - 2
  pf(qf(1 - gpower_inputs$alpha, df1 = 1, df2 = df_error),
    df1 = 1, df2 = df_error, ncp = 2 * n_per_group * f^2,
    lower.tail = FALSE)
}
# Search whole-number group sizes and select the first meeting target power.
anova_n <- function(f) {
  candidates <- 2:1000
  candidates[which(anova_power(candidates, f) >= gpower_inputs$power)[1]]
}
# Compare correct f with incorrectly entering d in the f field.
gpower_correct_n <- anova_n(gpower_f)
gpower_wrong_n <- anova_n(gpower_d)
gpower_actual_power <- anova_power(gpower_wrong_n, gpower_f)
```

```{r gpower-effect-sizes, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Calculation = c("Two-sided independent-samples t test",
    "Equivalent two-group one-way ANOVA",
    "ANOVA with d mistakenly entered as f"),
  `Effect-size input` = c("Correct: d = 0.60", "Correct: f = 0.30",
    "Incorrect: f = 0.60"),
  `Analyzable per group` = c(ceiling(gpower_t_plan$n), gpower_correct_n,
    gpower_wrong_n), check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Required analyzable patients per group for a 3-unit target difference and SD 5: correctly specified effect sizes and a mistaken input. All calculations use a 5% Type I error probability, 90% target power and equal allocation.")
```

Entering $0.60$ in the $f$ field makes the software plan for a difference twice as large as intended: 6 units instead of 3. The resulting sample of `r gpower_wrong_n` patients per group would have approximately `r round(100 * gpower_actual_power)`% power to detect the intended 3-unit difference. The difference observed in previous data and clinical threshold are unchanged.

The sample sizes in Table \@ref(tab:gpower-effect-sizes) were calculated in R using the corresponding noncentral t and F distributions and rounded upward to equal group sizes. They exclude recruitment losses. In G\*Power, the matching procedures are *Means: Difference between two independent means (two groups)* under *t tests*, and *ANOVA: Fixed effects, omnibus, one-way* under *F tests*. Both use an *A priori* calculation; the t test uses two tails and allocation ratio 1, while the ANOVA uses two groups.

Before using a result, you should check that the selected procedure matches the planned analysis and that each input has the meaning the software expects. Recording the target difference and SD in their original units makes the calculation easier to check. The [methods and software record](#tutorial-methods) explains what to retain.

For a planned analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), baseline adjustment introduces further assumptions about how the covariates relate to the outcome and how much variation remains after adjustment. The effect-size input should reflect that analysis. The simple $f=d/2$ conversion above applies to the stated unadjusted two-group comparison. The FDA's guidance discusses planning and prespecifying covariate adjustment [@fda2023covariates].

render_error_activity("software")
```

## Validating a sample size calculation {#validating-calculations .advanced-heading}

Before a calculation enters a protocol, it should be checked against an independent implementation or a published worked example using the same method. This is especially valuable when an unfamiliar procedure produces a number that is difficult to judge from experience. For open source software, the documentation, source code, tests and version history make these checks possible. A package's availability alone provides little information about how thoroughly its particular procedure has been checked. Commercial software also requires the correct procedure and settings [@gpowermanual2023; @pass2022].

The check should cover three questions:

1. Does the procedure represent the planned study? The outcome, independent or paired observations, allocation, hypothesis and analysis should match. The input scale matters, as the [Cohen's d and f example](#gpower-assumptions) demonstrates.
2. Does the result behave as expected? In the basic comparisons, a smaller target difference or higher target power requires more patients when other inputs stay fixed. For a single-proportion normal calculation, halving the margin of error multiplies the unrounded sample by four. Per-group counts, total counts and recruitment allowances should be checked separately.
3. Can the number be reproduced? A second calculation should match the inputs, tails, approximation, continuity correction and rounding. Any remaining discrepancy should be explained before the result is used. For a complex design, simulation of the planned analysis can check power and false-positive probability, with enough repetitions to quantify simulation uncertainty.

The following calculations were run in G\*Power 3.1.9.7 and PASS 2022 version 22.0.8 on 25 November 2026. The two-group calculations use equal allocation, two-sided tests, a 5% Type I error probability and 90% target power. Counts are analyzable participants, before recruitment allowances. The G\*Power precision cells are marked “Not compared” because these checks used PASS's dedicated confidence interval procedures.

| Tutorial example and procedure | Tutorial result | G\*Power procedure and result | PASS 2022 procedure and result | Interpretation |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Two proportions, 60% versus 30%, pooled score test planning approximation | 56 per group, 112 total | z tests: Difference between two independent proportions, no arcsine transform or continuity correction. 56 per group | Tests for Two Proportions, Normal Approximation, Z-Test (Pooled). 56 per group | Matching methods agree. Calculated power after rounding is 90.165% in all three implementations. |
| Same two-proportion inputs with a continuity correction | Uncorrected tutorial: 56 per group | Same procedure with continuity correction selected. 62 per group | Not compared with this setting | The correction changes the calculation. The extra six per group reflect a method choice. |
| Two means, difference 3, common SD 5, pooled two-sample t test | 60 per group, 120 total | t tests: Difference between two independent means, d = 0.60. 60 per group | Two-Sample T-Tests Assuming Equal Variance. 60 per group | Matching methods agree, with calculated power 90.312% after rounding. The teaching normal approximation gives 59 per group because it treats the SD as known. |
| One percentage, anticipated 20%, 95% confidence, full width 10 percentage points | 246 total | Not compared | Confidence Intervals for One Proportion, Simple Asymptotic, two-sided, width 0.10. 246 total | Matching normal approximations agree. The width at this count and the assumed percentage is 9.997 percentage points. |
| One mean, SD 5, 95% confidence, full width 4 units | Normal illustration: 25 total. App's expected t-interval width: 26 total | Not compared | Confidence Intervals for One Mean, unknown SD, distance to limits 2. 27 total | PASS holds the entered sample SD at 5. The app averages width over the sample SD's normal-sampling distribution. These are different width criteria. |

Table: (\#tab:software-validation) Direct software checks of the tutorial's basic calculation examples. Exact procedure names and settings are retained in the [validation record](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/documentation/software-validation.html).

For the mean example, the app's expected full width is approximately 3.999 units at 26 observations. PASS's full width is approximately 3.956 units at 27 observations when the sample SD is fixed at 5. The normal illustration uses a $z$-value of 1.96 and gives 25. These differences can be understood from the stated methods [@pass2022].

A useful validation record retains the original inputs, software versions, both outputs and the reason for agreement or disagreement. For open source functions, the saved test should be rerun after a relevant code or package update. Agreement supports the numerical implementation. Whether the assumptions represent the intended study remains a scientific question.


```{r consider-software-difference, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_consider_check("consider-software-difference")
```

## Protocols and supporting records {#reproducibility-record .advanced-heading}

The reproducibility record is the collection of materials needed to check the calculation: inputs and their sources, methods, software versions, code or saved settings, results and dated decisions. It can be stored alongside the study protocol and statistical analysis plan (SAP). The UMCG SAP template is one component of this collection.

The study protocol sets out the design and objectives. The SAP specifies the analyses in enough detail to implement them. Their outcome definitions, sample size assumptions and primary analysis should agree. The [UMCG SAP template](https://umcg.zenya.work/document/2f52710d-3ebc-495e-a4dc-6dee95742c78) supplies a structure for this record [@umcgsap].

The sample size calculation report should retain the evidence and reasoning behind each numerical input, alternative scenarios and dated amendments. A revision should identify what changed, why, and what information was available when the decision was made. The [software record](#software-record) and [simulation record in Chapter 6](#simulation-reproducibility) specify the computational details to preserve alongside this scientific reasoning.

<details class="advanced-explanation" id="complex-design-record">
<summary>Additional records for complex designs</summary>

For the [testing strategies in Chapter 7](#multiple-outcomes-comparisons), the protocol and SAP should also specify the following items where relevant [@iche91998; @fdamultiple2022; @fdaadaptive2019; @umcgsap]:

- The primary and key secondary outcomes, treatment comparisons, success rule and family of confirmatory claims, including their testing order and error-control procedure.
- The number and timing of interim analyses, information used, efficacy or futility boundaries, safety review arrangements and who has access to unblinded results and makes decisions.
- The sample-size re-estimation or other adaptation rule, its trigger and limits, and the corresponding final testing and estimation methods.
- Maximum and expected sample sizes under stated scenarios, with the planning method or simulation used to evaluate false-positive probability, power and other relevant performance measures.
- The dated protocol and SAP versions, software, code and inputs needed to reproduce the decisions, and a record of any amendments and the information available when they were made.

The [UMCG SAP template](https://umcg.zenya.work/document/2f52710d-3ebc-495e-a4dc-6dee95742c78) includes sections on significance and multiplicity, interim analyses and changes from the protocol. In the [report activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/assumptions_report/?stage=review), the planned analysis, software and conclusion fields can identify the design-specific plan, supporting documents and unresolved decisions. The [annotated core report](#write-a-sample-size-justification) remains a worked example for one comparison and a final analysis.

</details>

<details class="advanced-explanation" id="uncertainty-calculation-details">
<summary>Calculation details for the uncertainty example</summary>

The [worked uncertainty example](#further-planning-approaches) uses R's normal power approximation for the frequentist probabilities. For the Bayesian analysis, independent binomial likelihoods update Beta(1,1) priors to Beta(1 + relief count, 1 + no-relief count). Numerical integration gives the posterior probability of benefit. Summing over all possible count pairs gives the probability of exceeding 97.5% under each planning scenario. There is no Monte Carlo error in this enumeration.

```{r uncertainty-helper-source, eval=FALSE, code=readLines("../R/uncertain_planning.R")[1:34]}
```

</details>

## Methods used in this tutorial {#tutorial-methods .advanced-heading}

Table \@ref(tab:tutorial-methods) distinguishes the planning calculation from the analysis of simulated data. Equal allocation and independent observations are assumed in the basic two-group examples. Differences are treatment minus control; their units and direction should be explicit.

| App or example | Planning or calculation procedure | Analysis or interval procedure |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Two proportions | Normal approximation using R's `stats::power.prop.test()`, two-sided with `strict = TRUE`; required patients rounded upward per group | The reasoning lab uses a two-sided pooled [score test](#score-test) without continuity correction and a Newcombe-Wilson interval for the difference |
| Two means: calculator and reasoning lab | Pooled two-sample t-test planning using `stats::power.t.test()`, two-sided with `strict = TRUE`; required patients rounded upward per group | Pooled-variance t test and t interval; R analysis uses `t.test(..., var.equal = TRUE)` |
| One population: lab estimation mode | Smallest total sample meeting the expected one-sample t-interval width for a mean, or Wilson interval width at the assumed percentage | Normal samples with one-sample t intervals, or binomial samples with Wilson intervals; the report records coverage and interval-width attainment |
| One population percentage | Normal approximation for the requested margin of error; the unknown-percentage option uses 50% for planning | A simulated binomial count is summarized with a Wilson interval |
| Sampling distributions | Normal probabilities for one sample mean with a known population SD | Rejection boundaries and probabilities follow the selected one- or two-sided rule |
| Recruitment adjustment | Optional switching multiplier $1/(1-a-b)^2$, followed by division by each group's retained fraction; the larger requirement is rounded upward once and used in both groups | Assumes complete switching and little variance change; equal recruitment with potentially unequal expected retained counts. It calculates requirements without generating patient outcomes |

Table: (\#tab:tutorial-methods) Statistical procedures used by the tutorial's calculation and simulation apps.

The score test and Newcombe-Wilson interval use different constructions, so their decisions at the null need not coincide exactly. A comparison across software should match the test, interval method, sidedness, allocation, correction and rounding rules. The [statistical methods documentation](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/documentation/statistical-methods.html) describes implementation details and limitations.

## Reproduce or adapt an example {#reproduce-or-adapt-the-examples .advanced-heading}

You can begin with [Activity: Simulate repeated neuropathic pain trials](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/book/simulation.html#activity-pain_simulation). After running a scenario, you can save its replications and assumptions, sample size calculation report and R script using the lab's download controls. The script loads shared functions from a repository checkout, so that checkout's commit should be recorded alongside it.

A practical reproduction follows these steps:

1. The source checkout should match the recorded code version. Its documented environment should be restored before running the saved script.
2. Saved inputs should match the result being checked, including sample size, population assumptions, test settings and simulation repetitions.
3. The saved script should run from the repository root. Its summaries can then be compared with the exported result using unrounded values where available.
4. Any changed method, software version or assumption should be documented before interpreting differences in the output.

For a compact example of the binary repeated-study algorithm:

```{r algorithm, eval=FALSE}
# Load the tutorial's analysis functions from the repository.
source("R/sample_size_functions.R")
# Make the random draws reproducible when rerunning this script.
set.seed(20260921)
# B is the number of trials; n is the number of patients in each group.
B <- 5000
n <- 100
# Generate each trial's number with relief directly from a binomial distribution.
treatment_count <- rbinom(B, n, .60)
control_count <- rbinom(B, n, .30)
# Analyze each pair of group counts with the same test.
results <- analyse_binary(treatment_count, control_count, n, alpha = .05)
# Estimate power as the fraction of trials with p < .05.
mean(results$p_value < .05)
```

Adaptations should keep the editable R Markdown, shared case settings, app code and build instructions together. You should review changes to assumptions and methods alongside the resulting figures and activities. The [adaptation guide](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/teaching/adaptation_guide.html) provides practical steps [@bothmann2021].

## Your own study {#own-study .advanced-heading}

<span id="extend-study-plan"></span>

In [your continuing report](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/assumptions_report/?level=advanced&stage=question), the detailed prompts expand the same answers into a fuller sample size calculation report. Under *Study settings*, selecting relevant design features adds prompts for clustering, repeated measurements, survival outcomes, noninferiority or equivalence, multiple claims, interim decisions, or simulation. An external calculation can be documented with its inputs, method, result and software version. You can appraise evidence for each input, justify plausible ranges, compare several sensitivity scenarios, and document feasibility and unresolved decisions. Switching views preserves your writing and attached calculations.

Your study report can include a simulation result with its generating assumptions, analysis, repetition count and Monte Carlo interval. Your explanation should address what it adds to the analytical calculation. You can also write a short hypothetical study abstract that distinguishes the planned design, realized results and interpretation, following the broader learning sequence used in DICE [@thiesmeier2024].

Your project may involve estimation, a fixed dataset or dependent observations. The [study-design guide](#study-designs) should inform your choice of method. In [Activity: Build your own study calculation](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/power_explorer/?activity=own_study), you can assess plausible assumptions and resource limits, then explain whether to proceed, collaborate, redesign or narrow the question. The [reproducibility record](#reproducibility-record) should accompany the result.


<div class="chapter-recap">

### Take-home points {.unnumbered}

- Computational reproducibility uses the same inputs and procedures; replication investigates the same question with new data.
- Software and its settings should match the planned analysis, including the meaning and units of each input.
- Independent calculation checks should match the procedure and inputs, with any discrepancy explained.
- A calculation record should include assumptions, methods, results, rounding rules, and software and code versions.
- A simulation record also needs data-generating assumptions, the analysis, the number of repetitions, and random-number settings.
- Complex designs also need their success rule, interim and adaptation decisions, final analysis and dated protocol/SAP versions.
- Sharing protocols and code supports checking and reuse. Data access should respect consent, confidentiality and other applicable restrictions.

</div>

# Test your understanding {#exercises .unnumbered .reference-heading}

The discharge exercise provides optional practice with basic calculations. The cumulative quiz brings together the tutorial's main decisions, with explanations and links for review.

## Additional practice: discharge percentages {#discharge .unnumbered}

In this optional practice, you compare three sample size plans for the same hospital-discharge trial. The aim is to see how a relative increase differs from an increase in percentage points, and how the target difference and target power affect the number of patients needed.

Suppose a hospital is planning a trial of a new discharge-support program against standard care. The outcome is discharge within seven days of admission: yes or no. With standard care, 80% of patients are expected to be discharged by then. All values in this example are hypothetical.

Each plan specifies its target difference. All three use equal group sizes, a two-sided test, a 5% Type I error probability, and no allowance for losses at this stage.

| Plan | Target difference | Target power |
|:--|:--|:--|
| A | A 20% relative increase from the 80% standard-care percentage | 80% |
| B | An absolute increase of 10 [percentage points](#percentage-points) | 80% |
| C | The same target difference as Plan A | 90% |

Table: (\#tab:discharge-task) Three plans for the hospital-discharge trial, each using a 5% Type I error probability and a two-sided comparison.

The draft sample size calculation report below compares the three plans. Some passages need correction.

```{r discharge-error-review, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_error_activity("discharge")
```

You can check each plan using the [two-proportions method](#two-proportions) or [Activity: Discharge percentages](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/power_explorer/?activity=discharge). In the app's *Settings*, the standard-treatment percentage stays at 80%. The novel-treatment percentage and target power should match the plan. The *Overview* shows the required sample size per group. Each count is rounded upward before doubling for the total.

<details>
<summary>Show the calculation and interpretation</summary>

```{r discharge-answers}
# A relative increase multiplies 80% by 1.20; an absolute increase adds .10.
discharge <- data.frame(
  scenario = c("20% relative increase", "10 percentage points", "Higher power"),
  control = .80, treatment = c(.80 * 1.20, .80 + .10, .80 * 1.20),
  power = c(.80, .80, .90))
# Recalculate for each treatment probability and power target.
discharge$per_group <- mapply(function(p, power) {
  sample_size_two_proportions(p, .80, alpha = .05, power = power)
}, discharge$treatment, discharge$power)
discharge$total <- 2 * discharge$per_group
# Show per-group and total counts with probabilities formatted as percentages.
knitr::kable(display_probabilities(discharge, c("control", "treatment", "power")),
  caption = "Analyzable discharge-study sample sizes using the normal planning approximation in power.prop.test().")
```

The treatment percentages are 96%, 90% and 96%, giving target differences of 16, 10 and 16 percentage points for A, B and C. The approximate totals are `r paste(discharge$total, collapse = ", ")`, respectively. Plan B needs more patients than A because its smaller target difference is harder to detect at the same power. Plan C needs more patients than A because it aims for higher power at the same difference. Of these three plans, B requires the most patients.

Figure \@ref(fig:discharge-grids) shows how the relative increase in Plans A and C and the absolute increase in Plan B translate into discharge percentages.

```{r discharge-grids, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=5.3, fig.cap="Discharge percentages in illustrative groups of 100 patients. A 20% relative increase from 80% gives 96%; an increase of 10 percentage points gives 90%. The grids display assumed percentages; the sample size calculation determines how many patients the study requires.", fig.alt="Three grids of 100 squares. Standard care has 80 discharged and 20 not discharged. A 20% relative increase adds 16 discharges, giving 96 of 100. An increase of 10 percentage points adds 10 discharges, giving 90 of 100."}
draw_discharge_grids()
```

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-percentage-points">
<summary>Common misconception: a 20% relative increase in an event rate equals an increase of 20 percentage points</summary>

From a baseline of 80%, a 20% relative increase gives 96% ($0.80\times1.20=0.96$), an increase of 16 percentage points. An increase of 20 percentage points gives 100%. The baseline and whether the change is relative or absolute should be clear before you enter probabilities into a calculator.

</details>

</details>

The [discharge simulation app](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/power_explorer/?activity=discharge) examines how the approximation performs when the assumed event probability is close to 100%.

## About this resource {-}

This tutorial builds on Katalin Tamási’s original e-learning module [@tamasi2021]. Its presentation and three simulation activities draw on chapters 1, 11 and 15 of *Power Analysis with Superpower* [@superpowerbook2022]. Hans Burgerhof’s *Statistics 3: Sample size calculation* e-learning module informs the discussion of testing and estimation goals [@burgerhof2020], with further statistical background from @kirkwood2003, @whitley2002, @pourhoseingholi2013 and @wang2020.

Our account of developing the epidemiology and medical statistics e-learning environment describes the learner and teacher needs underlying this approach [@wieringa2025]. Evaluation emphasizes explanations, application to new cases, and usability feedback, since access counts and time online may not reflect learning [@chan2019]. The tutorial uses R Markdown [@allaire2021rmarkdown] and bookdown [@xie2021bookdown]; the build environment records the versions used for the current edition.

Except where otherwise noted, original teaching materials are shared under [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/) and original code under the [MIT License](https://opensource.org/license/mit). The [reuse and citation guidance](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/documentation/reuse-and-citation.html) explains attribution and third-party exceptions. Shared adaptations of the teaching materials must use the same or a compatible license.

## Further reading {-}

For communicating numerical findings, Gigerenzer and colleagues discuss transparent health statistics, and NICE recommends absolute risks with explicit denominators and time periods [@gigerenzer2007health; @nice2021shared]. Frequency formats and frequency trees support Bayesian diagnostic reasoning [@gigerenzer1995frequencies; @binder2021frequencies]. These principles inform the examples and the critical-appraisal learning outcome, expressed using revised Bloom's taxonomy [@krathwohl2002taxonomy].

Your choice of reading can follow the decision you need to make; the [reading guide](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/documentation/reading-guide.html) connects these sources to the activities.

- @fong2026 and @zrineh2026 introduce clinical planning; @lakens2022 explains alternative sample size justifications; @cook2018delta2 supports choosing and reporting a [target difference](#target-difference). Apply these to the sample size calculation report.
- Design-specific guidance: @ying2025 and @eldridge2016 address pilot objectives; @candel2023 addresses efficient designs; @riley2020 addresses prediction-model development. CONSORT's explanation and elaboration details reporting, including sample size assumptions in item 16a [@consortee2025].
- For multiple outcomes and testing hierarchies, see @fdamultiple2022. For interim analyses, stopping guidelines and sample-size re-estimation, see ICH E9, Sections 3.4 and 4.4-4.6 [@iche91998], and @fdaadaptive2019. These support the [testing strategies](#multiple-outcomes-comparisons) and [additional reporting checklist](#complex-design-record).
- For the distinction between an observed significance boundary and planned power, see @lakens2022 and section 1.7 of *Power Analysis with Superpower* [@superpowerbook2022]. Chapters 11 and 15 of that book extend the simulation examples.
- Further methods and reference books: @pargent2024 explains mixed-model simulation, and @superpowerbook2022 supports exploring repeated studies. @julious2004 reviews normal-outcome trial calculations; @julious2023 provides broader design-specific sample size methods. @piantadosi2024 places planning within broader trial methodology. These books offer further detail on design-specific methods.

For readers exploring prediction models, @shamsutdinova2026 describes recent simulation-based approaches (currently in preprint).

For specialized designs, @vembye2024 provides guidance and the POMADE R package for power analysis of meta-analyses with dependent effect estimates. @dey2026 develops calculations for sequential multiple assignment randomized trials (SMARTs) with skewed outcomes. These sources provide further reading on specialized designs. @marks2026 complements the Bayesian planning methods with evidence about their use and reporting in trials.
